speechtext:
On Tuesday last the hon. member for Yukon asked if I would make a statement in respect of the agreement which has been reached with the state of Alaska for keeping open the Haines cut-off highway. As he knows, this originated out of the sending of a group of senior officials from various departments to study the entire communications system in that area, which is becoming so important to northwest Canada.
I wish to inform the hon. member now that a senior official of my colleague the Minister of Public Works has proceeded to Alaska and has concluded an agreement with the state of Alaska to keep open our portion of the Haines cut-off road in British Columbia this winter at a cost of $127,050 payable in United States funds, for which the state of Alaska will furnish the equipment and the operators for the tractors, snowplows and so on. The government of Canada in the person of the Minister of Public Works will be providing the supervisory personnel.
When Mr. Williams of the Department of Public Works was there he also saw the minister of highways for British Columbia, Mr. Gaglardi, who had indicated prior to September 30 that his government would contribute toward the maintenance of the highway. However, he has indicated now that he would prefer to wait until after this experimental season is over, and if the operation is successful his government will be glad to contribute in the coming years.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAIN- TENANCE DURING WINTER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of what the minister has said in his announcement, am I to understand that the agreement that has been arranged has been concluded on the basis that the Canadian government is going to pay $127,050 for the rental of United States equipment and the wages of United States labour to maintain a Canadian road?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAIN- TENANCE DURING WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised that my hon. friend, who took full credit for the success of this project some time ago, should now find fault with it. As he well knows, and as I am sure many members of the house do not know, because of the particular and highly unusual nature of the geography of the area it would cost

many times more than the amount I have referred to if Canadian equipment were made available. speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
In presenting the estimates of the Department of National Defence to the committee for the first time, I should like, at the outset, to make reference to the ministers who were responsible in recent years for presenting the estimates of the department when I myself was sitting on the other side of the chamber.
I am sure members will recall the outstanding services performed by Major-General Pearkes, now His Honour the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia, and in the more immediate past, those of the hon. member for Calgary North.
Both of these gentlemen carried out their duties as ministers of national defence with distinction and I am sure that in so far as the hon. member for Calgary North is concerned, members will join with me in the hope that he will have an opportunity to take part in our discussions, since with his experience in office and notwithstanding any criticism he may feel obliged to make, his views on the important subject of defence will be greatly appreciated. I realize, Mr. Chairman, that normally in view of the large sums of money involved and of the significance of the subject matter, concerning as it does our national security, the house would expect a detailed
5454	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence statement from me at this time. However, in so far as these estimates are concerned, special conditions apply.
In the first place, they were prepared by the previous administration, and although some changes in detail have been made, to which I will refer later, they are in concept essentially those put forward by the previous government. Second, as hon. members know, we are now in the ninth month of this fiscal year and, in consequence, a large part of the money allocated to the department has already been spent.
A third consideration, and I think a very important one, is the fact that a special committee on defence has been established by parliament and since June of this year has been actively considering various aspects of defence. The committee has received statements from the service chiefs, from the chairman of the defence research board, from myself and, in addition, has called witnesses, both in Canada and abroad, from outside the department. Minutes of the defence committee, of course, have been available to all members and I do not want to take up the time of this committee in repeating information which is already on record in those minutes. The 1963-64 estimates which you are now being asked to approve, are required to carry out our present defence obligations.
Wherever members of our forces are involved in implementing these obligations, whether it be in the Congo or the Middle East in support of the United Nations, in Europe, on the high seas on behalf of NATO, or elsewhere here at home and overseas, they are carrying out their duties in the highest traditions of those who have served in the Canadian forces throughout our history in peace and in war. I am proud, indeed honoured, to be associated with the men and women of our navy, army and air force, who I feel are second to none in the world.
The members of this house, particularly those who have visited the forces serving abroad, who have observed their work and who have had the opportunity of talking with the international commanders with whom these forces are associated, will know at first hand of the high regard in which they are held. In Europe, they have quite rightly earned the reputation as "The Elite Corps" of the NATO forces, and the same high standard applies wherever they serve, in Canada and around the world. I am sure that all members of the house would wish me to say these few words of tribute to the men and women who serve Canada so well in our armed forces.
One of the reasons for the high calibre of our forces is the training received by young officer cadets in our service colleges. As hon.


members know, the Glassco commission had something to say about these colleges and, in fact, recommended closing Royal Roads. The advisory board of the colleges has carefully considered this recommendation of the commission and has submitted the opinion, with which I am heartily in accord, that the colleges are performing a necessary function having regard to the special nature of education and training required, the needs of the armed services and the current competitive situation in Canadian universities.
Royal Roads is an integral part of the Canadian service college system and the advisory board of the colleges, in expressing their views, recognized this fact. An educational institution is only as good as its teaching staff. At the end of the last academic year 56 per cent of the arts and science faculty at Royal Roads held doctorates, and this percentage will have increased to about 62 per cent by the end of the current academic year. This staff is active in research, in professional societies in Canada and abroad. Among other awards, one of the faculty was the only Canadian to receive a NATO research scholarship this year and another was the first Canadian in several years to receive a major award from the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique. The quality of the teaching staff has been reflected in a reducing failure rate: The rate for first year students is down from 20 per cent to 17 per cent, and the record of Royal Roads students in the third year at the Royal Military College is down from 17 per cent to 11 per cent. This is a very good record of achievement, and in recognition of the importance of this establishment, I state here that I agree with the opinion of the advisory board. Therefore, Royal Roads will not be closed.
Wherever our forces are serving, it is our concern to give them adequate equipment to carry out the assignments to which they have been committed. That has been the undertaking of successive governments over the years and, in general, Canadian servicemen on active service have been furnished with such equipment. There is one area, however, which is of immediate concern: This is the requirement to convert the truck-mounted motorized units of our brigade in Europe to armoured carrier-mounted, mechanized units.
To meet this requirement, a vehicle known as the Bobcat has been under development in Canada since 1954. At that time there were no competing United States or British developments and it was hoped that successful completion of the Bobcat development would result in a wide export market for the manufactured vehicle. Now, nearly 10 years later we find that the development

of the Bobcat has not yet reached a stage where the vehicle could go into production.
The contract for the manufacture of 20 pilot-production vehicles required the contractor to subject the first carrier produced to a 2,000 mile endurance trial. The vehicle failed to complete this trial successfully. As a result, further redesign work is required so that we are now faced with the fact that, even if no further delays occur, delivery of production vehicles could not commence before late 1965 nor be completed before the spring of 1967. I might add here that the foreign produced content of the Bobcat is approximately 28 per cent of the total, and the estimated production cost per model has increased to a very considerable extent over the original estimate.
In the meantime, the M-113 armoured personnel carrier similar to the Bobcat, has been developed in the United States. The M-113 has been in service for three years and has been adopted by several of our NATO partners including Denmark, Greece, Italy and Germany, as well as a number of other countries outside NATO. From the logistic point of view, this is of considerable importance. Important too is the fact that the Bobcat would cost per unit close to double that of the M-113.
In view of all these circumstances, and bearing in mind the urgent requirement of the brigade, the government has decided to terminate work on the Bobcat program and to meet the brigade requirements by procurement of the M-113 carrier.
Parts of the M-113 for the United States production are already being manufactured by Canadian sub-contractors, and through the production sharing arrangement with the United States, further sub-contracting in Canada of a variety of equipment can be anticipated.
As hon. members, especially members of the special defence committee who are here today know, a review has been under way within the Department of National Defence to determine the best and most effective contribution we can make to the collective defence of the free world and to the maintenance of peace in the years ahead. This review is proceeding and some preliminary decisions have been made, following studies in particular fields; relating to equipment programs which, if proceeded with, would seriously limit the determination of what our policy may be in the future. With rapidly changing concepts of warfare and improvements in weapons technology, I think most hon. members will agree that such a review is not only desirable but essential.
In addition to the work we are carrying out, I am looking forward to receiving the
Supply-National Dejence interim report of the special committee on defence which, I understand, will be submitted to the house later this month. As I have stated previously, I expect to be in a position to table in the house a white paper on defence next year, prior to the consideration of the 1964-65 estimates.
In so far as the estimates for the current fiscal year are concerned, these, as shown in the blue book, amounted to $1,590,006,537 and I think it would be of interest to hon. members to give some breakdown of this amount in addition to the details contained in the blue book. Personnel, operating and maintenance costs account for 77.3 per cent of the total; major equipment 16.6 per cent; construction 3.1 per cent; development 1.0 per cent; mutual aid 2.0 per cent.
The ratio between maintenance and capital costs is a matter of concern which has been, and is being given serious study within the department. Our aim is to find ways and means of reducing overhead, and by cutting operations and maintenance costs, achieve a re-direction of expenditures to improve our defensive capability. This is not a simple task. It requires an intensive study of alternative ways to achieve our purpose, and careful cost-effectiveness analysis of the components of the defence programs. This is clearly a process requiring continuous and constant attention.
Without this careful attention-call it judicious pruning, if you will-our defence budget would soon top the $2 billion mark if we were to maintain our present establishment, with all its ramifications, and at the same time furnish our forces with adequate equipment and weapons. It is our intention to keep defence expenditures within reasonable bounds, without affecting the true operational effectiveness of our contribution to collective security.
Our end objective is to get the best result for each defence dollar spent. To do this, it is essential to examine critically each element of the defence program in terms of its cost and its contribution to effective defence.
Over the last several months a thorough examination has been made in a determined effort to appraise whether the dollars going into the various components of our defence organization are producing appropriate results. We have now reached a number of conclusions which will result in reductions in expenditures for maintenance of the defence establishment. This is an essential first step towards providing, in the longer run, a more effective contribution to the national security of our country from the resources that can be made available for this purpose.
These changes do not materially affect the estimates you are being asked to approve

There is no way of accomplishing these worth-while re-adjustments without causing some individual and community problems. We are therefore anxious to give the maximum advance notice of changes in order to minimize these problems of re-adjustment.
Speaking first of all of the Royal Canadian Navy, our examination has shown us that costs can be reduced in some areas. The navy now operates about 160 auxiliary vessels of various kinds such as tugs, supply ships, harbour craft, and so on. We find that we can take 10 of these vessels out of service, the majority by March 31, 1964, and continue to support the operation of the fleet adequately.
We have also examined the utility aircraft squadrons on the east and west coasts and we propose to reduce these by six fixed-wing aircraft and two helicopters before the end of this fiscal year. These squadrons are engaged in support functions such as target towing, transportation of personnel and so on.
An examination of the ammunition storage depots has led us to the conclusion that the naval ammunition depot at Kamloops, British Columbia, can be closed, and the ammunition stored there re-distributed to other depots.
We propose as well to close the naval supply depot at Lynn Creek, British Columbia. This is a stores depot that has been used by the navy and also in part by the army. The functions can be re-distributed to other units with a saving in overhead costs.
The naval armament depot at Longueuil, Quebec, is to be closed as the essential functions of this depot can be carried out at the naval establishment at Ville Lasalle at a considerable saving in costs. The navy has maintained a naval repair facility at Point Edward naval base in Sydney, Nova Scotia, and this repair facility will be discontinued but the navy will continue to operate the stores depot and record centre at this location.
It is also the intention to discontinue the naval activities at Fort Pepperrell, Newfoundland. The navy has provided the housekeeping of this establishment and this has been a costly activity in terms of its present defence capabilities.
It is anticipated that most of these changes will be completed by March 31, 1964. However, it is not planned to have any of the reductions in ship repair work at the Point Edward naval base take place until after the beginning of the new fiscal year on April 1, 1964. This will ensure that operations at the naval base are gradually reduced after that


date in relation to the development of alternative opportunities for employment. There will be adjustments involved for some of those now employed at this base. In order to assist, efforts will be made to organize training and re-training programs in co-operation with the provincial government wherever these will be suitable. Other measures will also be introduced as appropriate in the circumstances. These changes should produce in a full year, once they have been implemented, savings estimated at $7,750,000.
Turning to the army, an announcement has already been made regarding the transfer of the northwest highway system, effective April 1, 1964, to the Department of Public Works. At that time the Department of Public Works will assume responsibility for employment and it is expected that the majority of the present civilian employees will be retained.
Also, as I have intimated to the house, we intend to withdraw personnel from Fort Churchill, Manitoba, in 1964 at which time administrative responsibility will be taken over by other government departments.

speechtext: All army personnel?

All army personnel. It is expected that most of the civilian personnel, numbering 346, will be taken over by other government departments assuming responsibility for administration at Churchill. The rocket responsibility facilities at Fort Churchill will be continued. It is also intended to close the army vehicle depot at Hagersville, Ontario. Dispersal of vehicles to meet command and national survival requirements is now under way and should be completed by April, 1964. The balance of the vehicles will be moved to other army units, including London, Ontario, during the period May to October, 1964. Civilian personnel now at Hagersville will not be released until the vehicle movement program has been completed. These changes, when fully implemented, will result in an annual saving in operating costs to the army approximately $16 million.
As far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned, adjustments include the withdrawal from Churchill, which I have already mentioned, and Resolute Bay, where in both cases responsibility for airfields will be transferred to the Department of Transport; the cessation of fixed-wing aircraft activities at Rockcliffe airport; the transfer of the electronic warfare unit from St. Hubert to Uplands; and the transfer of responsibility for St. Hubert airfield to the Department of Transport. These changes will be effected in the spring of 1964.
What about Penhold?

The R.C.A.F. station, Calgary and No. 10 repair depot, Calgary, will be closed as early as possible in 1964; the buildings will be declared surplus to Royal Canadian Air Force requirements. The disbandment of No. 107 search and rescue unit, Torbay, Newfoundland, and the closing of R.C.A.F. station Torbay will be completed by the spring of 1964, although the R.C.A.F. radio station will remain. The deletion of one band by the spring of 1965 has already been announced. The air photographic section of the R.C.A.F. photographic establishment, Rockcliffe, will be transferred to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys as soon as the necessary arrangements can be made. Royal Canadian Air Force stations Vancouver, Saskatoon and Hamilton will be closed early in 1964, with the search and rescue school and composite unit, now at Vancouver, being transferred to Comox. In a full year these changes are expected to reduce operating costs by about $8 million.
A review has also been made of the requirement for the reserve forces. The reserve forces of Canada have traditionally been maintained as a mobilization base for active service formations, for providing reinforcements for regular force units, and for filling positions not required except in an emergency. In recent years they have had the added role of assisting in civil survival in the event of a nuclear attack on this country. We have looked at the reserve force organization as it now stands, with the object of determining realistically the support which reserve formations can provide in an age when combat readiness is a key-note of defence power. This has led to the conclusion that the reserve forces of all three services can be reduced from the present levels.
The reserves of the Royal Canadian Navy now comprise 21 divisions and two reserve air squadrons with a current strength of approximately 4,000. To meet those needs of the Royal Canadian Navy in an emergency which could be, we believe, satisfactorily met by reserve forces, it has been concluded that a strength of approximately 2,700 is required. As a result it is proposed to close out seven naval divisions and the two air reserve squadrons. The reserve air squadrons are located at Toronto and Victoria. The reserve divisions which are to be closed are those at Prince Rupert, Victoria, Edmonton, Regina, London, Charlottetown and Halifax. I should add that the Charlottetown division will not be closed out next year because of the centennial celebrations taking place in that province.

The tender at Kitchener will also be closed. It is planned to reduce the militia to a strength of approximately 30,000. The militia now has a strength of 51,000. This will necessitate a major re-organization of the militia. The militia is now organized on the basis of a very large number of units in the various army corps essentially, as I have said, based on the traditional concept of a substantial mobilization base. This organization for example includes 26 regiments of the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps, 29 field regiments, six medium regiments and a number of independent batteries of various types in the Royal Canadian Artillery, seven field regiments in the Royal Canadian Engineers, and so on. Hon. members will agree that a re-organization of this magnitude is both important and complicated and must necessarily take account of the regional interests across this country taking part in and supporting the militia. We will be appointing shortly a select group of militia officers from across Canada who will be asked to examine this problem and to make recommendations as to the way in which this re-organization should be brought about.
The R.C.A.F. maintains a reserve with a current strength of approximately 2,200. The air force, by the nature of its responsibilities, must be maintained constantly in a state of immediate readiness and there are few areas in which support from the reserves would be necessary in an emergency. It is planned to reduce the R.C.A.F. reserves to a strength of approximately 860. This will retain in the reserves six auxiliary flying squadrons and their associated wing headquarters. The auxiliary squadrons at Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon and Hamilton will be closed out early in 1964. The six squadrons that are being retained are located at bases which serve other R.C.A.F. purposes and the costs associated with these are consequently very much less than those at the squadrons which are to be closed.
The changes in the Royal Canadian Navy and Royal Canadian Air Force reserves are expected to result, when they have been fully taken into effect, in savings in operating costs of about $5,250,000 a year. The savings resulting from the re-organization of the militia are expected to be very considerably in excess of this, but until the details have been worked out I am not in a position to give a figure. It would, however, be of the order of magnitude of about one third of the total now spent on the militia. The total now spent is about $45 million a year. Some changes are proposed in our regular force structures. As these involve consultation with our allies I am not in a position to announce

It is the capital votes that have been largely affected in recent months. These include the cancellation of the general purpose frigate program and the decision to reduce the number of additional CF-104 dual aircraft to be procured from 24 to 16. On the other hand, preliminary funding is now included for the purchase of three Oberon class submarines and for the construction of storage facilities for nuclear warheads required to make effective weapons systems previously obtained. There is one other item which is not reflected in the estimates of the department, but is of some importance, and that relates to the decision of the government to increase armed services pay and allowances and the salaries of class "D" employees retroactive to October 1, 1962.
The estimated cost of these revisions for the 18-month period ending March 31, 1964, amount to just over $43 million, but since no provision was made for this expenditure in the 1963-64 defence estimates, this is being financed by means of allotments from the Department of Finance general salaries vote. In addition, there was a supplementary estimate of $827,000 for the defence research board satellite program.
In these brief remarks it has not been possible to discuss wide areas of our activities. As I stated earlier, the special committee has studied many of these at some length. My remarks today have dealt with current housekeeping changes. In each case careful thought has been given to the possible effect on future policy, and in each case it has been concluded that the proposals do not limit the range of possible policy options which might


be considered by the government. I am sure hon. members will prefer to leave the policy discussion until the special committee has reported and the government has had a chance to study that report. However, if there are any specific questions which would aid hon. gentlemen in their deliberations, either the associate minister or myself will note them and provide the information requested at a later stage in the debate.
At this point I would like to pay tribute to the associate minister. On the basis of an understanding between us, he has been carrying the bulk of the administrative load in the department. He is one of the hardest working members of the administration, and without his assistance a general review of the kind we have undertaken would have been impossible. I do hope that his invaluable contribution will be fully recognized. I would not like to conclude without saying that the associate minister and I are both appreciative of the wonderful co-operation we have had from all members of the department since we took office.
Finally, may I say that it is a matter of some regret that these announcements must be made now in advance of the tabling of the white paper and the presentation of the government's defence policy. As a result an incomplete picture is available which can only be completed at a future date. Decisions had to be taken in order to permit the preparation of estimates for next year, and on careful reflection it was considered that the interests of the people affected overrode other considerations, and with this in mind, immediate announcements should be made in order to give maximum notice and opportunity for readjustment. Consequently, we have decided in favour of human considerations and followed the course which provides the maximum notice possible under the circumstances.

I thought, Mr. Chairman, that at this stage, after eight months in office, the Minister of National Defence would have given us, as former ministers of national defence have done under similar circumstances, a statement of the policy of the government. This government was to be the government of decision, the government that was to tell us what was wrong with the past and what they were going to do for the future. Eight months have now gone by and all we get is a housekeeping account from the Minister of National Defence. I think he should turn in his housekeeping keys and hand the job over to somebody else. Surely we should have had at this stage some statement of general policy on the part of this government. We heard from these people sitting opposite us that no statements of policy were made while we were in office. I have gone to the trouble to look back and see the statements made in the past, statements published by General Pearkes in 1960 and by the hon. member for Calgary North when he was minister of national defence. Yet here we are faced with this minister who, in the course of his eight months in office, has made no statement of policy in this house on the part of this government with regard to national defence. That is a shocking neglect of duty.
A great deal was made by the minister earlier this year when the session opened in May, and again when it was resumed in the fall, about the question of nuclear arms, the so-called commitments which our government, he alleged, had entered into and how they were going to deal with these matters, and deal with them promptly. These planes were to have been armed immediately so that they could play their part in the defence of the North American continent. Again, I point this out: eight months have gone by and not one step has been taken to correct this so-called deficiency.
How do we stand with regard to our air division in Europe, the force which has been called the elite among our defence forces as far as the air is concerned and I accept that description? Is it ready to take action if war should break out today or tomorrow or next week? Is one single plane of the air division ready for action? Is one single plane of that division, on the quick reaction alert station, in position, with a nuclear bomb attached to the undercarriage? Let the minister answer if one single plane is thus equipped. He will have to say, first, that the air division is not yet complete and that it will not be complete as to the total number of planes, until the spring of next year. He will have to admit he has done nothing about the squadrons which either are, or may be, stationed in France, without any nuclear equipment. And he will have to admit that the squadrons presently in Germany have no nuclear bombs available immediately for action at the present time. Eight months have gone by and nothing has been done by the Minister of National Defence in this regard.
I suggest there has been no occasion since the days of the Liberal government in 1939 when the Canadian air force has been less able to take action in war than at the present moment. Members opposite talked about unpreparedness. This is a shining example of unpreparedness, and it is typical of the Liberal regime in that period of the 'thirties, in 1939 and 1940. Here we see the same crowd, or their successors, carrying on the same attitude as was shown then. Our great air division


in Europe is unable to do a thing. Last May I asked the Prime Minister how many planes were then ready for action and how many were ready in April of this year. The Prime Minister replied-and this answer will be found in Hansard on page 114: "Not one, because they need ammunition". I say, now, to the Prime Minister, and to the Minister of National Defence, that not one is ready today -because they need ammunition. Except for the period up to 1939 I do not know of any period in Canadian history when we have been less prepared for action in the event of an emergency. This is a shocking state of affairs.
Let me ask the minister this question: Why did he discontinue that part of the air division in Europe which was equipped with interceptor planes and which had been active for a number of years? Why did he discontinue all of this force before he was ready with the Starfighters equipped for action. He wiped them out. Only two or three weeks ago I was at Murviel in France. There was not a fighting plane in action there. This was not the case for years, previously. We had effective interceptor forces, the elite of the air force in Europe. But at the present moment there is not a fighting plane at Murviel and Starfighters elsewhere are not equipped for an active role.
The Minister of National Defence cannot excuse himself. He carries a heavy responsibility. The people of Canada are relying on his assurance that our defence forces are ready at a moment's notice to take action. But that is not the situation at the present time. As to taking effective action, we are in worse shape than we were a year ago, because the air division in Europe then was equipped with interceptors; the changeover was just commencing. Now the hon. gentleman has let the whole thing collapse and there will be a lapse of several months yet before the air division is ready to fight. Even then, unless he makes some arrangement with regard to the bases in France, he will not be able to equip a full half of that air division.
This is not good enough. We have given this government an opportunity. We have given it a chance. People have said: Let them get on with the job and demonstrate what they can do. Well, how long do they need? I suppose, a year, or a year and a half. We are to have a white paper some time in January or February. We do not know when the house will meet again. I will hazard a guess that we shall not see that white paper until late in February. Then we shall have a statement on defence policy. Perhaps.

This is not enough. The people of Canada have, up to this moment, been relying on the Minister of National Defence to provide adequate defence for this country. The people of Canada have, up to this moment, considered that our forces were now ready to fight. Well, the air division in Europe is not ready to fight, and the Bomarc sites in Canada are not ready for an emergency, and the Voodoo planes in Canada are not equipped with the nuclear missiles which the present minister said were so essential if they were to fulfil their role. Second, although there are other points on which we may criticize the minister, I think we should commend him for having the courage after eight months in office to make announcements on these estimates regarding housekeeping which should have been made a long time ago, and which if it had been done before would have saved millions of dollars of the Canadian taxpayers' money.
It is only peanuts for them.

My hon. friend says "peanuts", but it runs into millions of dollars. I am prepared to commend the minister for his courage in announcing the housekeeping arrangements which he has under contemplation.
It is impossible in the time allotted to me to comment on all the various aspects of defence raised by the minister. I shall have to proceed, therefore, as speedily as possible with what I had in mind, and which I believe deals with defence policy.
In that connection I must say first of all, as is well known, there are 24 members of this house who are members of the special committee on defence. We have been meeting since last June, sometimes in camera, not only here in Ottawa but also in Colorado Springs and in Europe. Whenever we had a special meeting in camera the chairman of the committee always opened the in camera meeting with one statement, that we could always use the information as long as it was not attributed to the particular source. I want to make that clear because in discussing defence policy one must use some information.
I want to say, and I say it on behalf of the New Democratic party, that in our estimation there has never been a Canadian defence policy under any government in peacetime which took into consideration the part that Canada could or should most efficiently play in the military world on behalf of the democratic countries. I want to go even beyond that, Mr. Chairman, and say that we strongly feel that

the defence policies of all governments in the past in peacetime have been governed by political expediencies and economic pressures, rather than by an understanding of the part that Canada could or should play. To that, sir, I add my third point, that Canadian defence policy has been based on misinformation supplied by civilian and military authorities, not only in Canada but in NATO and in SHAPE. This is something of vital concern to Canada.
I only want to give one illustration of what I mean by "misinformation". Over the past few weeks many of us in this house have been hearing how policy in Canada, NATO, SHAPE and various countries, is based on the Soviet threat, on the fact that within a matter of weeks the Soviets could have between 165 and 174 divisions in the field. Right up until November 23, we in the defence committee of this house were being told that by civilian and military authorities. However, we find that on November 18, while SHAPE or other ministers were giving us that information, the United States secretary of defence, Robert McNamara made a statement in New York. I am not quoting from a newspaper; I am quoting from a copy supplied by the United States information service, supplied to me by the embassy here in Ottawa. What is this statement? I quote:
Recent intensive investigation has shown that the number of active Soviet divisions that are maintained at manning levels anywhere close to combat readiness is less than half of the 165 and the 175.
We have the United States secretary of defence making a statement like this on November 18, and one week earlier and later we were being told by the military people in Europe that it is 165 to 170. You understand now why I say I am afraid there is flim-flam, balderdash and misleading statements being given to the members of NATO, SHAPE and Canada.
I should like also to raise a matter which I believe is of major importance to all members of this house. I am not going to do this on a partisan basis; but, I am going to remind all members that in the early days of this session there were many counterchallenges and charges between the Prime Minister of today and the Leader of the Opposition of today, as to whether or not Canada had made a commitment on nuclear warheads and nuclear weapons. In recent weeks I think we have found the answer. Both are right and both are wrong. The information is now available and it can be found on the records of our special committee, to the effect that the NATO council has never at any time discussed what a commitment is as it concerns the 15 member nations of NATO. I quote the answer, because I asked the question:

A commitment starts with plans submitted by military authorities to governments. Ministerial meetings give approval. This constitutes a commitment, but is not a binding contract. The exact meaning of a commitment has never yet been discussed in the NATO council.
I think that information should have been given to this house in the early days of the discussion at this session as to whether or not Canada was committed by a binding contract to nuclear weapons and to nuclear warheads. I should like to put a question in this way. It is time for honesty in Canada, NATO and SHAPE as to what defence policy is in Europe, what defence policy is in Canada. May I just remind the members of this house that we are in NATO. We have 6,500, approximately, in our brigade and we have 6,500 in our air force. In the last five years we have paid, for these 13,000 armed personnel under NATO in Europe, no less than $350 million a year and as high as $436 million-that is for these 13,000 active Canadian personnel. Why is this so? It is my belief that it is mostly from a psychological point of view. However, they are there.
They are called the elite, and I believe it. Everybody told us how wonderful and, sir, if you want to check the report you will find it complete. I cannot mention names, but included are NATO, SHAPE, and our own representative. I will just give one quotation, "It is conceivably true that Canadian forces in Europe are short on mobility." You find in the records from NATO and SHAPE over-emphasis on nuclear tactical weapons and under-emphasis on conventional.
You will find, sir, if you check the record, and it is an official record, that Canada is in a strange situation. We have 6,500 men in a brigade which is not mobile. I ask why?
I was at the NATO meeting in 1961 and was a member of the scientific and technical committee. We put forward a unanimous recommendation that we all get together and stop wasting money on duplication of research and production. Some 24 of us were in Europe two weeks ago, and we were told on the highest authority that in many cases, in the absence of political expediency and economic pressure, military equipment could be produced for less than one third of what NATO had to pay for its military equipment.
This brings us to the situation in Canada where we have got to face it too, politically and economically, whether we are interested in a Canadian defence policy and Canadian defence purchases, or whether we are interested in political and economic pressures, and to hell with what it costs the taxpayers of Canada. If we in Canada are not prepared

Supply-National Defence to face up to that issue, how do we expect that the NATO council is going to face up to it?
We in this party continuously and consistently have opposed Canada becoming a part of a nuclear club, with the acquisition of nuclear weapons and nuclear warheads. Anyone who reads the entire text of the speech made by secretary of defence Robert S. McNamara, on November 18 in New York, will find paragraph after paragraph of evidence of the need for building up conventional forces, highly mobile, and he also made a most important statement to the effect that he does not anticipate a war will break out in Europe.
War might break out in African or Asian countries, and if it does then comes the need, not for a NATO force with nuclear, tactical weapons, but for highly trained, fully mobile forces, which will answer one request, that is, the suppression of brushfire wars throughout the world; and this can only come under the United Nations.
I see my time is drawing to a close, so in conclusion I wish to say I regret we have not seen any publicity in our Canadian press during the past year concerning the fact that three Scandinavian countries have got together and have reached agreement on highly trained, mobile forces to be placed at the disposal of the United Nations as a police force for the world. Only three days ago I found out that in two of these Scandinavian countries this policy is going to he referred to their parliaments for adoption, following which an official offer will be made to the United Nations.
Surely Canada should have given the lead in this regard? Even though we are late now, I believe we should get together with these three Scandinavian countries who have this enlightenment and understanding, and then have a real Canadian defence policy that will enable us to play our part on behalf of maintaining peace throughout the world. This demands that we have an idealistic and factual Canadian defence policy so we can play our proper role for the peace of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity of participating in the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. There is an increasing interest in the importance of this subject, and this is both healthy and understandable when viewed from a number of points; first, the tremendous amount of money involved in the carrying through of the responsibilities of the department, second, the fact that it involves the welfare of thousands of Canadian servicemen and servicewomen and,

third, it is something that has to do with the very survival of Canada and the free world.
At the beginning of my remarks I would like to refer to the statement made by the Minister of National Defence, which has been characterized as a housekeeping report. I believe it does indicate the fact that serious attention has been given to a number of items, sometimes of lesser or greater significance, but items that should receive attention. With regard to the statement made by the spokesman of the official opposition that he expected the minister to make a statement of government policy, may I point out that the minister has been considerably kicked around in past weeks because of the fact that he has been anticipating the report of the special committee on defence. Therefore it is rather unusual that on an occasion like this he should be criticized if he fails to come out and make definite defence policy statements.
I. prefer to confine my remarks to general statements because I do not want to anticipate the report that will be brought in by the defence committee, of which I have the privilege and honour to be a member. There is widespread questioning of the adequacy of our defence program, and I believe a general feeling that we are not getting our money's worth as far as this essential program is concerned. While sympathizing with the minister and his officials in the task of trying to plan effectively in a field where changes are so rapid and far reaching, we hope the minister's program of rethinking and reviewing defence policy will result in some basic and much needed dynamic reforms.
A statement appeared in a periodical some time ago. I am not going to quote it because unfortunately it was just a sheet taken out of a periodical and I have not on the sheet the name of the periodical or the date. But it was very critical of the defence department because, instead of getting down to it and facing realistically the problems of the present day this article suggests the department is made up of those who are writing or rewriting United States and British defence reports. If that has been true in the past, and if it is true today, then surely we must come to the point of recognizing the need for a new look at and a facing up to the changing situations that exist in this particular field.
The Minister of National Defence himself was apparently very unhappy with certain aspects of the defence program. He called attention to the fact that as far as our NATO commitments and our forces overseas are concerned he was not satisfied that we were

in a position to discharge effectively the tasks to which we have been committed. I think one of the most significant moves to meet the situations in the realm of defence was pointed up in the appointments of the special parliamentary committee on defence. We are very happy about this; it was something we had anticipated, and the leader of our group suggested that this particular defence committee be set up. It is a matter of record that we presented this suggestion in certain campaigns. We were therefore very happy that the Prime Minister saw fit to introduce legislation setting up this defence committee, because I believe it has fulfilled and will fulfil a very important task in this particular field of activity and study.
I believe there are several aspects of our defence program that must be covered and will be covered by the inquiries conducted by the defence committee. I know that sceptics belittled the proposal, and in fact I remember one of my opponents pointing out that it was inconceivable that a group of politicians would be able to sit down and work out, in a spirit of harmony and co-operation, a policy that was adequate for Canadian needs and present day conditions. I think the activities of this committee have indicated that it is possible for a committee to work in this particular way, and as we look back over the work of the committee I believe it will prove eminently worth while in the setting up of proposals relative to national defence. As has been pointed out by other speakers, we have made a number of inquiries here in Canada. Our inquiries have also taken us to Colorado Springs and North Bay, and we have had a great many sittings right here in Ottawa. We spent two weeks overseas visiting defence establishments, listening to briefings by government leaders of the various nations comprising NATO, and we have been briefed by the military authorities of those nations as well as by the leaders of the collective defence organizations of the free world.
The work of this committee is still incomplete; there is still a great deal to be done. But I believe, as I have said, it will accomplish a great deal in the setting out of worth-while guide lines for the minister's information as he endeavours to set a course with regard to national defence for this country. One of the encouraging aspects of the work of the committee was, I might say, the complete absence of political partisanship. I am hoping this particular attitude will prevail not only as far as the committee is concerned but as far as parliament is concerned as we endeavour to set out what we believe to be adequate defence policy for
Union Trusteeship Correspondence this country. I have said before, and I say again, that this is too important an issue to be dealt with in the political, partisan arena. This was kept in mind in the setting up of the committee. The view was that it could be lifted above political partisanship and we could arrive collectively at some policy that would be adequate to meet the need in this field.
I would suggest it is highly improbable that the government, having had this committee set up, would consider lightly or would ignore the recommendations that without question will be forthcoming. As has been stated, the work of this committee has been carried on conscientiously and diligently with an almost complete lack of political consideration. We are expecting the government in turn to accept the recommendations that are given, in the spirit in which they have been formulated and will be formulated, and will give very careful consideration to those recommendations that will be forthcoming.
I have promoted among the members of the committee, and perhaps among the public generally, the idea that the committee work should not be confined to just this one particular session but should become something more permanent, in order that the valuable information secured and the work carried out will be able to assume a degree of continuity that will be of assistance to the minister and his department in this vital field.
Canada's defence policy must cover three very important areas; first of all, our own national territory-and what a stupendous task this is.

Mr. Speaker, in the wink of an eye or the brief flash of a second in which I had the opportunity to speak when this matter was first brought up for discussion some weeks ago I indicated to the house that I should like to enter into a discussion of the principles involved in connection with the production of diplomatic correspondence such as that called for by the notice of motion presently before the house. I also indicated that I should like to make specific reference to certain precedents which had been cited to the house, and make a few observations on parliamentary practice in general. The position I should like to take is not exclusively related to the particular correspondence or the particular diplomatic negotiations between Canada and the United States concerning the great lakes; it is related to the status of diplomatic correspondence generally.
My first argument is that a compulsory revelation of diplomatic correspondence in response to a private member's notice of motion for production of papers would have an adverse effect on the good conduct of Canada's diplomatic relations. My position would be that not only would such a motion embarrass Canadian diplomats and the Department of External Affairs in its negotiations with foreign parties, but it would have an adverse effect on the country as a whole.
The first argument to which I would direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that above all it is desirable to have complete candour of discussion in diplomatic intercourse and correspondence. Indeed, if the art of diplomacy and the conduct of diplomats have been the subject of any criticism in this century it is because in the public's eye, at least, there has been a lack of candour. I suggest that it is desirable, in international negotiations and relations generally, that the diplomats representing various nations be able to deal with each other with the same candour as any two contracting parties in a commercial transaction-perhaps even with a greater degree of candour if that is possible.
At the same time I would point out that the private candour which diplomats might show in such negotiations between themselves may frequently be too blunt for public discussion. What I mean to suggest is that the field of discussion between diplomats may prove to be too strong meat if it is to be unreservedly placed before the public. Direct embarrassment in international diplomacy
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
might result if at any particular time negotiations with foreign parties or, extending the principle even further, discussions between the foreign offices of two particular nations, should at any time be forcibly revealed to public gaze under the compulsion of a motion such as this. I think the reasons for that are quite clear to all hon. members. I think it is quite clear that the publication of communications from a foreign country to this country, and this country's replies to such communications, and vice versa, may well embarrass the foreign country concerned in its dealings with its own citizens.
I do not think it requires much by way of example to indicate that there may be times when a foreign government might be prepared to discuss a particular position, or a particular move or treaty, for which it might not have prepared its own subjects. The compulsory disclosure of such negotiations, or even the suggestion that that particular country should make such correspondence available for its own citizens, might well result in a political storm in the country concerned. Equally, I submit that undue exposure of diplomatic correspondence might embarrass such foreign country in its dealings with third parties or its allies.
May I take an extreme example merely for purposes of illustration and remind hon. members of the adverse effect to the country concerned of the accidental disclosure of the Zimmerman telegram in 1917, which, perhaps more than any single incident in that particular spring, became a direct factor resulting in a state of war between the kingdom of Germany and the United States. It is quite clear that, as in the case of the Zimmerman telegram, if communications between party A and party B which make reference to their relations with party C are forced out onto the open, a step which the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) is taking in moving a motion such as this-although I am not suggesting here that any third parties are involved- then, embarrassment, although not on the scale of that resulting from the disclosure of the Zimmerman telegram but which nevertheless would be considerable, could injure the foreign country concerned in its dealings with other contracting parties and allies.

I am talking in terms of the general principle that the disclosure of

diplomatic correspondence might prove highly embarrassing to any country involved in diplomatic negotiations with Canada. Therefore, I point out to hon. members to whom this fairly obvious fact does not seem to have occurred, that motions of this kind, which would provide essentially the means of forcing into the public record these particular communications, would have the inevitable result of making foreign powers less candid in their dealings with this country as well as in their international negotiations. We are fortunate internationally in having a great many allies; there is a very friendly demeanour toward Canada in international circles. It would therefore be a great pity if those friendly relations were to be put in jeopardy, and the candour one would expect from friendly nations prejudiced, as a result of action taken by members of this parliament to disclose to the public diplomatic negotiations which might thereby result in embarrassment to the particular country involved.
Nor, I suggest, contrary to what some hon. members have indicated, is this a matter, as it is with regard to the provinces, of merely asking for foreign consent to the disclosure of these documents. I know that on occasions it has been done, but I believe even this procedure entails distinct diplomatic disadvantages which could inconvenience Canada in its foreign relations. For one thing, the mere act of withholding consent by a foreign power could be misconstrued and result in suspicion as to the motives for withholding that consent. It could, indeed, result in suspicions which might go far beyond the merits of the particular question involved. These are reasons, I submit, why the house should continue to recognize the long established principle that confidential diplomatic correspondence should not be made available in response to motions of this kind.
I should like to refer in this connection to the views of an outstanding foreign diplomat, Mr. Jules Cambon, a distinguished member of the French academy in his monograph "The Diplomatist". He observes at page 27 of the English version:
Last of all, a negotiator must observe discretion, and indeed it is no more than his bounden duty to do so, not only for the sake of his chief but of his fellow-negotiator as well. Negotiations partake of the nature of a conversation, and neither of the principals is at liberty to make even the smallest disclosure without a grave dereliction of duty towards the other. You can make things very awkward for your opponent by showing up his hesitations, his offers, and his various twists and turns; but you will often defeat your own ends by doing so and almost certainly ensure the breakdown of negotiations.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I thank my hon. friend from Essex West for the opportunity of putting some of these principles before the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue who appears never to have heard of them before. But to continue my quotation-we are referring to intriguers:
It is they who by bruiting abroad whatever information they succeed in obtaining undermine the authority of those in charge of the negotiations and impugn the good faith of the government they claim to be serving.
I am submitting that it would be against the interest of the Canadian government to hamper Canadian diplomatic negotiations by accepting a motion of the type put forward by the hon. gentleman. I should like to refer

to a number of outstanding authorities who would support this proposition. I suggest, in particular, that the proper view of these circumstances is that the executive, in other words, the government, must retain the power to decide in any particular case whether confidential documents such as these would, if revealed, result in harm being done to the public interest. If the government does so decide, then the house should recognize the need for taking such a decision and the issue should not be pressed. In support of this contention I should like to refer to the second edition of Todd on Parliamentary Government in England. As hon. members will recall, the learned author was the distinguished librarian of the parliamentary library of this house. He observes, at page 356:
It Is unquestionably of immense advantage to the country that the diplomatic transactions and proceedings of government abroad should be freely communicated to parliament. .. .But a certain amount of discretion must always be allowed to the government in respect to communicating or withholding documents and official correspondence which may be asked for by either house of parliament. While it is necessary that parliament should be informed of all matters which are essential to explain or defend the policy of government, it is equally necessary that a minister should be able, upon his own responsibility, to withhold from the public such information as he may judge could not be afforded without detriment to the public service. Ministers are sometimes obliged to give "extracts'' only from official papers, in certain cases; but parliament is bound to receive what is communicated upon the faith and credit of the administration in whom their general confidence is reposed, unless they are prepared to question the personal integrity of ministers, or to pronounce a verdict of censure upon their public conduct.
And continuing later:
Thus, it is generally inexpedient, and highly impolitic, to communicate to parliament papers concerning diplomatic negotiations which are still pending; and "nothing is more prejudicial to the action and efficiency of the diplomatic service than the perpetual motions for the production of papers, which are made by a certain class of politicians", who insist upon the fullest information on questions of foreign policy, at unseasonable times.
Then, at page 359:
Any attempt to coerce the government into producing to parliament all the papers they may possess upon a matter of foreign policy, without regard to their being confidential, or unsuitable for general publication, could only result in compelling the agents of government to have recourse to "private correspondence" for the communication of everything but mere ordinary information. This would occasion not only immediate public loss, but also permanent injury to the state.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the privilege at this time to rise for the purpose of putting forward reasons for the consideration of my colleagues why this motion should not be adopted. As a month has elapsed since the motion was last considered I think it would be useful at this time to read it again. It is in these words:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of all telegrams, correspondence, communications and other documents and replies thereto between the government of the United States of America, or any of its departments, and the government of Canada, or any of its departments, concerning the great lakes shipping situation and the proposed trusteeship of Canadian maritime unions since the 6th of July, 1963.
When the hon. member proposed this motion some weeks ago he raised certain arguments in support of its passage. I should like to take this opportunity to comment on them briefly. First, the hon. member referred to certain press reports of comments of officials of the United States government on the issue then concerning the two countries, the United States and Canada. I gathered that he in effect said that, by reason of these officials making these comments to the press, in a sense the privilege ordinarily attached to such documents might be considered to be waived and there was therefore no grounds for withholding the documents from the house on the basis of the arguments of lack of consent, in effect, of the neighbouring government of the United States, and of public policy.
May I suggest to the house that there was no suggestion in the press reports or, more important, in the arguments put forward by the hon. member that the words of these United States officials were in any way quotations or summaries of any of the documents which the hon. member seeks to have produced through his motion. I have read his remarks with some care, looking for some evidence contained in them that the references he made to quotations from the press and, in fact, words of ministers of the crown in this house with respect to these comments were in a sense quotations or extracts made by these officials from documents of the United States government or any of its departments or instrumentalities. Certainly in the remarks of the hon. member on the last occasion this motion was debated we find no such evidence.
I think the principles to be applied here are basically two. One arises out of the fact that 28902-5-349
Union Trusteeship Correspondence the correspondence, tabling of which is requested, has passed between two governments, our own and that of the United States of America. The other is linked to the question of public policy and the public interest. I think the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) has brought forward some valuable and useful precedents to indicate the problems that arise when documents are exchanged in the course of diplomatic negotiations between two sovereign states. I think it is clear that it would certainly be most inappropriate, if the other sovereign state in question should not indicate its consent or desire for the tabling of the documents in question, for this house to pass a motion which would in effect compel the government to table the particular documents. We have no indication that the government of the United States of America would be in the least way willing to have these documents brought before us.
I think the hon. member for Rosedale put before us quite a useful point in directing our attention to the fact that a new and in this case quite unnecessary cause of potential conflict between our two countries might be created, if it should happen that a motion of this type were passed compelling the government to produce the documents in question at a time when the necessary consent of the government of the United States had not been obtained, a consent which they might well consider to be most necessary involving as it does correspondence, documents, state papers, which in their view of the public interest, not only of their own country but the general mutual interest, are such that it would be better that the documents in question not be produced.
In the attempt of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) to bring before us some precedent he referred to the fact that on occasion international air agreements have been tabled in the house. He attempted to show that since these agreements were between two countries, the United States and Canada, and were documents involving two nations, and since they were tabled, this in effect created a precedent for the passing of the motion compelling the tabling of the documents which the hon. member seeks. In my opinion the precedent, if there is such, is not relevant to the situation. In fact, I would go further and suggest it is not really a precedent at all because in discussing the motion before us what we are talking about is not a document involving a final conclusion, a final agreement, the entering into of some type of final accord between

Union Trusteeship Correspondence two nations but rather the preliminary documents that have embodied in them and reflect negotiations that might lead up to some type of final agreement.
I think it is clear it is not the customary practice, especially in matters as delicate as the one out of which this motion has developed, to bring before the house the documents which the hon. member seeks under a motion of this type.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the only effect of bringing these documents before us would be to help make more difficult the solution of the problem out of which this particular motion has arisen. In making this comment I am not implying that I have personal knowledge, which I do not, of the contents of these documents. Each side might be referring to bargaining positions taken for the purpose of reaching some ultimate conclusion. The documents might contain certain factual information which, if generally made available to the public, would make it most difficult to reach some appropriate and final conclusion. It can easily be seen, I submit, how the presentation of these documents, which are really only preliminary steps in an attempt to reach some final conclusion, could be a most difficult and harmful thing when we are trying to solve the problem on which this particular motion is based.
Let me, then, turn to the ground of public interest which is relevant in considering whether or not the documents covered by this particular motion are such that their production should be compelled. I think that this is an occasion when, as often happens in assemblies of this type, events have overtaken the particular motion or question under which debate is taking place. If you read the motion you will see that it refers to the proposed trusteeship, and legislation in connection with it was passed many weeks ago. The first time the subject matter of this particular motion arose was October 31. I suggest, sir, that events have certainly overtaken the hon. member's motion. Since that time, the parliament of Canada has passed into law a bill setting up a trusteeship over the maritime union. The trustees have been appointed and have assumed their functions. They have taken over their duties and are carrying out those duties under the powers given to them by the parliament of Canada.
We find, too, that the emergency situation which seemed to be in existence at the time this motion was presented no longer seems to exist. Although we can readily admit there is still a problem of grave seriousness in the United States and Canada, shipping that has not already been halted by the onset of winter is being carried on from Canadian

ports. The wheat shipments we have undertaken to make to Russia and other countries are being carried forward. The problems that faced our Canadian ships in United States ports are not of the same intensity that they were some five or six weeks ago. While I think it is correct, as the hon. member has suggested when he presented this motion, that this is essentially a Canadian problem, it is one that we have to recognize transcends to a certain extent the boundaries of our own nation, since the waterways in question obviously are those through which the international boundary runs.
I think we can readily agree that it would be impossible to come to a final solution of the problem on which this motion is based without the co-operation of the United States government and the leaders of the United States labour movement. I would suggest to this house and to all hon. members, that at this point, when relative calm has descended on the troubled maritime transportation scene, nothing at all could possibly be gained by proceeding with this motion at this time. In fact, I suggest to the hon. member who presented this motion that if he is really as concerned with the public interest, as I am sure he is in respect of this matter, if he still feels, as I am sure he did at the time he moved this motion, that there is a grave question of public interest involved, it would seem to me that the way to serve this public interest at this time would be to withdraw this motion, to remove the opportunity for inadvertently re-opening at an inappropriate time a question which, if it is not closed, is at least not as troublesome as it was.
We had a situation which seemed to be on the verge of explosion. The maritime labour front situation at one time appeared to be likely to halt Canadian shipping and to spill over the boundaries of a friendly nation, thus troubling the labour movement in that country. This situation does not appear to have the same potential violence now. We can recall that there was a situation which appeared to threaten the friendly relationships, the links between the two labour movements in the United States and Canada. It would appear that at least temporarily, and we hope permanently, some type of accord has been reached between the two principals. We hope some understanding has been reached or is on the verge of being reached between our two governments on this important question.
I suggest again to the hon. member who proposed this motion that it would be the highest expression of action in the public interest to withdraw the motion and to remove even this slight risk of opening this question at a time when it is unnecessary. I suggest,

therefore, for a number of reasons this motion should not be supported by this house. First of all, I suggest the action of the United States officials in making comments to the press, and to which the hon. member who moved this motion has referred, were not quotations or summaries of official documents; second, I think it is clear that the public interest cannot possibly be served by revealing documents of this type, documents which as I have already indicated have been exchanged between the United States and Canada; and we have had no indication that the government of the United States has expressed any willingness whatever for these documents to be presented to this house.
So, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I not only suggest that this motion be defeated if it should happen to come to a vote, but that the only appropriate thing for the hon. member to do with this motion at this time is to withdraw it. We would give unanimous consent to that course, since this would be the highest expression of public interest on this very important question.
