speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May I advise the house that we are meeting again at seven o'clock. It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.

At five o'clock I was referring to three areas which must be considered when we are thinking of Canada's defence obligations. The first, of course, is our own national territory, and when we consider the geography of this nation, its immense area and the distance of its boundaries in relation to a population of just 19 million people we can appreciate what a tremendous task it would be to defend these shores. In these circumstances we recognize the necessity of forming alliances which would bring others to our assistance in the defence of our national boundaries, just as they would oblige us to help defend the interests of our friends.
The second area to which I referred is, of course, the North American continent as a whole and our obligations in this respect are covered to a large extent by our link with NORAD. There is, in addition, the contribution which Canada must make to the defence of the free world, and this contribution is made most apparent by our part in the NATO alliance. All this is a large order for a nation of 19 million people, but it represents a task we must face realistically and courageously. It may be we shall have to make a choice between providing a small and, possibly, inadequate contribution in many fields, on the one hand, and making an adequate contribution in a selected role on the other. This is a matter to which careful consideration will have to be given.
Canada has never shirked her responsibilities, and her efforts in the past have earned the gratitude of all her friends. The hon. member for Vancouver East has referred to the statements we heard while we were in Europe regarding the quality of Canada's forces and I am sure that those qualities will be recognized in the future, as in the past, by all those with whom we are allied.
I should like to take this opportunity of dealing with the question of our personnel stationed abroad. An article appeared in tonight's Ottawa Citizen entitled: "Hellyer plans to pare military attache posts". It has to do with the attitude of the Minister of National Defence toward certain of our personnel abroad. The article states, in part:
Supply-National Defence
It is reported that defence minister Hellyer was appalled when a manpower study he had ordered showed that Canada's 39 senior military attaches abroad draw annual living and rental allowances totalling $343,200.
Most of these embassy posts are filled by colonels or their equivalent in the navy and air force- captains and group captains.
The article draws attention to the obvious risk of overlapping which occurs, and points out that other officers in various areas could well undertake the responsibilities now carried by these attaches. It states:
A military attache is maintained in Paris, though dozens of Canadian senior officers serve at supreme allied headquarters there. He draws a monthly living allowance of $609 and a rental allowance of $247 on top of a monthly salary of nearly $1,000 excluding marriage and subsistence allowances.
While we were in London a question was raised as to the number of officers and other ranks attached to our missions there. We were told there were 52 officers, 47 other ranks, 348 dependants and 77 civilians. I repeat, there were 52 officers. I do not know, but it seems to me the situation we face overseas is the same as the situation which faces us right here in Canada: We have too many chiefs and not enough Indians. This may explain why our expenditures are so tremendously high in relation to the number of active personnel we have in the forces. It appears that the minister himself is unhappy over this situation, and no doubt he will be taking some action in relation to it.
I should like to return now to a statement to which I referred this afternoon. I refer to another statement made by the Minister of National Defence, this time to the Empire club in Toronto. I should like to quote from a report which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of November 28:
Defence minister Hellyer today admitted there are "serious problems" in respect of the Canadian army brigade and air division in Europe.
The minister said plainly that the brigade is not properly equipped to hold down its present advanced role with the NATO northern army group in Germany.
He said the situation of the R.C.A.F. air division, with half its strength in France where nuclear ammunition was not available, was simply not satisfactory.
Here again we find the minister very unhappy with the situation of our personnel abroad. Once again, speaking personally I would agree that the minister has some reason to be perturbed about this situation. When we were at Zweibriicken we had the opportunity of meeting the leaders of the third wing of our air division, and in reply to questions and through the contacts we made there we found that the air force was not in any way prepared to meet any kind of emergency that might arise. It seemed as

Supply-National Defence though they were completely without weaponry. They were vulnerable in every sense of the word. When we hear references made to combat readiness they certainly do not appear to apply in that particular respect.
As far as the army brigade group is concerned, some of the factors that were brought to our attention there indicated that they are very ill equipped to fulfil any essential and prominent role in defence. I am not saying anything whatsoever, Mr. Chairman, by way of reflection on the personnel of our armed forces abroad. I believe they are of the highest calibre and they are anxious and ready to do any job that may be assigned to them.
There were a number of officers and men who expressed themselves as being very happy that the defence committee set up so recently had seen fit to come to visit them and to investigate the contribution that they, representing Canada, were making. The particular role assigned to our forces abroad is not the important question to them, as far as I could ascertain. They expect such decisions to be made in Ottawa. But they are extremely anxious that their role be defined and communicated to them so that they can go ahead and be tops in the job with which they are charged. The morale is high but I believe that morale can only be maintained if our service personnel know what the job is and are given the opportunity to maintain peak performance and preparedness in the face of that responsibility. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is absolutely essential that policies must be forthcoming.
Reference has been made to the past months and past years when we have not had an adequate or effective defence policy. I say again that policies must be forthcoming. Decisions must be made. A reassessment is essential and action is imperative to give a sense of direction and to lay down the guidelines for the responsibility that we are accepting in the roles which we intend to fulfil.
As I stated before, I do not intend to anticipate the committee's report. I do not even submit personal views at this time with regard to defence policy. But with the tabling of the report of the committee and the outlining of its recommendations I believe it will be the responsibility of the government to prepare to move quickly and decisively in the adoption of a defence policy that will establish the role of our forces at home and abroad so that uncertainty will be ended and our forces enabled to reach the maximum standard of preparedness to fulfil their tasks.
It is true, as wa were reminded when overseas, that the era when war could be a continuation of foreign policy in another form


is over. War with our present destructive capability is, as we are all aware, too catastrophic to contemplate. However, I believe our defensive capability must be maintained lest any possible aggressor consider our unpreparedness a sign of moral weakness and use the opportunity afforded to further his own objectives. While respecting the minister's hesitancy in acquiring weaponry that might limit operations in the future, I believe it is imperative that no time be lost in defining our roles and then moving quickly to prepare to fulfil those roles to the maximum degree possible.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, I pay tribute to those who are serving in the forces abroad, and here at home, of course, but I am sure we all recognize that we must set the objectives and outline the roles. Without question, those in the forces are then prepared to go ahead and make their maximum contribution to the defence of Canada and the free world.

Mr. Chairman, we are considering the estimates of what I believe to be the most important department, namely the Department of National Defence. When you study the estimates for the various departments, you find that 25.6 per cent of the national budget is spent by the Department of National Defence, whereas only 19.1 per cent goes to social security and health, 5.3 per cent to veterans affairs, 4 per cent to transport and 1.4 per cent to unemployment insurance.
There is no need to say that when 25.6 per cent of a national budget is allocated to one department, its expenditures must be scrutinized, not only by the ministers but also by all the members of the house.
The estimates of the Department of National Defence amount to $1,560 million this year, after deducting the $74 million which were to be used for buying CF-104 and Voodoo CF-100 aircraft. And despite that reduction the expenditures will amount to 25 per cent of the national budget, while the estimates for natural resources and industrial development represent only 8 per cent and payments to the provinces, 5 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that this percentage of 5 per cent for the provinces could have been increased by acceding to the requests of the premier of the province of Quebec as well as those of the other provincial premiers.
The estimates of the Department of Agriculture amount only to 2.7 per cent of the whole national budget, while those for the unemployment insurance commission represent only 1.5 per cent, as I said earlier.

Mr. Chairman, among the larger estimates of the Department of National Defence, we see that $291 million are allocated to the Royal Canadian Navy, which is $24 million more than last year. Does this increase include the $30 million we will need to purchase submarines from Great Britain? The estimates do not say.
The estimates for the Canadian army amount to $444 million, that is $7,791,000 more than last year.
As for the Royal Canadian Air Force, its estimates amount to $691 million, that is $38,702,000 less than last year.
The estimates for defence research and development amount to $51,217,000, that is $8 million more than last year.
The estimates concerning mutual aid for NATO amount to $32.1 million, that is $4.8 million more than last year. The estimates for contributions and other allowances have been reduced by $2,720,000.
As I said a while ago, these various amounts make a total of $1,560 million, that is $30 million more than the previous year, despite the decreases announced this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence.
Mr. Chairman, what is most surprising to me is the detail of vote No. 1, which reads as follows:
Departmental administration including authority, notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, and subject to allotment by the treasury board, for total commitments of $2,529,570,600-
How much?

-$2,529,570,600 for the purposes of Votes 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 and 65 of this department regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment-
Now, the Department of National Defence is authorized to spend up to $2,529 million, an authorization that is actually granted, while these expenses will amount to $1,560 million this year.
Mr. Chairman, X wonder how it is that the Department of National Defence, which is authorized to spend up to that amount, does not allow, through a cabinet order, other departments to use that portion of its supply.
For example, why is the natural resources and industrial development division not allowed to use that supply which the Department of National Defence will not be using this year?
They are authorized to spend up to $2,500 million and only 8 per cent of the whole national budget is allotted to industrial development and to the development of our natural resources.
We could also allocate the amounts which will be of no need to the Department of
Supply-National Defence National Defence to other departments, so as to allow a more adequate development of all the riches and physical facilities we have in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the government might, for example, double the family allowances' rate; that would cost $1,040 million, half a billion less than what we are spending at the present time for national defence, and there would be one billion more that would circulate among Canadian families.
If old age pensions were increased by $10 a month, that is by $120 a year, for each of the one million Canadian pensioners, it would cost Canada $120 million. Instead of increasing income tax rates, the government could have used national defence estimates which the minister will not use this year any more than he did last year.
Under its contribution to joint programs, the federal government pays out $50 million: $30 million for old age assistance, $4 million for the blind and $16 million for the disabled. If those federal benefits were doubled, it would cost the government only $50 million. Here again, the necessary funds could be taken out of the estimates of the Department of National Defence which are not used at present.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to call the minister's attention to those cuts in expenditures as it seems to be done in other countries of the world.
This afternoon the Minister of National Defence gave clearly to understand that some radar stations would be closed in various locations in Canada in order to save the department approximately $74 million.
Some people have been employed in those radar stations for eight, 10 or 11 years and they are very worried following the statements made by the Minister of National Defence. There should be some co-ordination and agreement between the various departments so that when jobs are abolished or there are layoffs in a department, such as that of National Defence, another department would look after the workers deprived of their jobs. In such cases, I suggest that the departments of trade and commerce and industry should look after the matter or that they be authorized to spend the funds which will not be used by the Department of National Defence.
I will now quote an excerpt from La Presse of December 3, 1963:
The budget which will be presented by the Department of National Defence for the next fiscal year, will amount to about $1,560 million.
The $74 million reduction mainly stems from the decisions made by the minister of defence, Mr. Hellyer, not to buy other CF-104 atomic

-Following those decisions, estimates for weapons and equipment which were supposed to reach $279,441,000 fell to a new low for the decade. On the other hand, expenses for personnel, operations and maintenance continued to go up and reached more than $1,100 million.
That is just for salary increases and ordinary operations.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that some changes could be made in the estimates of the Department of National Defence. The report which was submitted to us last year on the expenses of the Department of National Defence and those of the Department of Defence Production clearly shows that the government and the two departments concerned make extravagant outlays.
I read in the issue of Wednesday, December 4, 1963, of Le Devoir, an article by Paul Sauriol which said:
Three days after the federal-provincial conference, a news report from Ottawa informed us that the Minister of National Defence had cut his budget for the current year by $74 million. The federal treasury thus recovers almost the equivalent of the $87 million it is giving to the provinces. There may not be any direct link between the two occurrences, but it is more than a coincidence, because many people feel that the most efficient and the most logical way to meet the requests of the provinces is to reduce considerably our defence expenditures.
It is true, several provinces, particularly the province of Quebec through Hon. Rene Levesque, suggested to the federal authorities to reduce expenditures for national defence in order to be able to give larger amounts to the provinces.
And he went on to say:
In spite of all that can be said with regard to our commitments to the Atlantic alliance and our share in the defence of North America, our military budget is too big, and it is the part of federal expenses which may be most easily reduced.
Mr. Chairman, when comparing our expenses with those of the United States, the difference is obvious.
And further on:
Those statements were illustrated by some figures:	The United States has more than 500
I.C.B.M. and will have over 1,700 in 1966, whereas the Soviet union only has a fraction of that figure. The United States has more than 500 bombers ready for action, which is twice the number which the Soviets would send as a first wave over North America. The same superiority exists with regard to the hundreds of I.R.B.M. So that, if anything more were to be done in the nuclear field, the point of diminishing returns would be reached...
...There is no more question of the old monopolies, the American nuclear monopoly or the Russian conventional forces monopoly. The west realized the limitations of the nuclear deterrent, and increased its conventional forces, but Moscow

also knows that an aggression with those conventional forces which would endanger the major interests of the west, in Berlin for instance, would bring about retaliation with tactical nuclear warheads. It is therefore a question of balance.
That is all Mr. McNamara said, but those who were listening could read the budgetary implications of his remarks between the lines. It meant that the new balance of forces might result in the reduction of some military expenses, more particularly with regard to nuclear arms; moreover, in order to reduce the deficit in the balance of payments, Washington may progressively decrease the importance of its forces in Europe, the more so as a recent experiment showed that a whole division could be transported by air in two or three days.
Therefore, if the military budget is notably reduced without jeopardizing the security of the country and of the west, the American government will have more ample resources available to stimulate economy, to modernize industry, to give a greater measure of assistance to emerging countries, to be more competitive on world markets, and to make up the deficit in the balance of payments.
In that light, Canada may hope to reduce also its disproportionate military effort, which absorbs one fourth of the federal budget. Even after the reduction which has just been announced, those expenses remain above one billion and a half. An energetic reduction of those exorbitant expenses would allow a better equilibrium between the federal and provincial finances. The hierarchy of needs would be easier to respect.
This amounts to what I stated a minute ago, that all the reductions in the national defence budget should be directed towards other divisions, such as that of the economic expansion of Canada.
If, in order not to weaken the armed forces of the country, we have to maintain our soldiers' pay, their standard of living, their jobs, it would be as easy, I think, to do so through building something in Canada instead of letting them exist in a passive way, as is the case now.
Those fabulous amounts should be devoted to the transfer of several thousand soldiers, if necessary, toward a direction other than that of national defence. So, it would be advisable, it seems to me, that those military men be directed towards the economic expansion of their country, instead of remaining in passivity or in a sort of idleness, as is the case now.
Mr. Chairman, we have here, under the heading of national defence, cases which are presented to us day after day. I feel I should call the attention of the minister to a statement from General Charles Foulkes of Victoria, B.C., who, speaking on national defence expenditures before the special committee on defence, the chairman of which is the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve), declared, on October 22, 1963, the following:
I am not convinced that we know really which antisubmarine force is the more effective and the most economical for Canada.

And the Minister of National Defence was announcing at that time the purchase of submarines at a cost of $30 million. General Foulkes said:
We are not convinced, we do not know exactly which would be the most effective and the most economical antisubmarine force for Canada.
There was never, as far as I know, an impartial estimation of the relative value of the aircraft carriers, scouting planes, frigates, submarines, helicopters and long range marine aircraft, to combat nuclear submarines. We have replaced the Magnificent by another aircraft carrier, and wartime frigates by relatively slow escort ships, at a cost of $30 million. (That figure would be obsolete today.) Lancasters have been replaced by Argus marine aircraft, and these will have to be replaced also in 1970. We are right in asking ourselves whether this present combination of an aircraft carrier with scouting planes, frigates, helicopters and long range marine aircraft constitutes the most effective, the most useful, the most economical combination for this job. I consider this combination rather as a conglomeration of plans and ambitions of the navy and air force organizers.
That is a statement by General Foulkes, a Canadian general who said boldly: The present arrangement is rather a collection of plans and ambitions by navy and air force organizers.
And now, here in the parliament of Canada, we are voting $1 billion, possibly $1J billion for national defence or something which amounts to a collection of plans, instead of an effective defence in case of attack, need or necessity.
Mr. Chairman, the Department of National Defence spends 5.6 per cent of the total national budget. Out of those fantastic expenditures, we still see the Department of National Defence treating people in the most arrogant manner you could think of.
I have a case here which dates back to 1951 and was discussed before various ministers of national defence, not necessarily before the present minister, but before the ministers of past administrations.
I am referring to the Senneterre radar station, in the riding of Chapleau, which was established in 1951. At the time of the establishment of that radar station, the government decided to take over claims which properly belonged to a mining prospector of the city of Val d'Or whose name is Joseph Lavoie.
Mr. Joseph Lavoie was the owner, since 1950, of mining claims located on the present site of the Senneterre radar station.
He asked the Department of National Defence for compensation. On several occasions, he was asked to report to the latter, or to send his claim to the Department of Transport, and afterwards to the Department of Industry, and then again to the Department of National Defence, and later still to the Department of Defence Production. He was sent from post to pillar since 1950, without ever getting any compensation though he was
Supply-National Defence the owner of that mining claim which is the present site of the Senneterre radar.
Here is for instance, a letter dated 1957, written by Mr. George Hees, the then minister of transport, to Mr. Andre Begin:

Dear Mr. Begin:
This is further to my letter of November 15 in connection with the effect of crown requirements on property owned by your client, Mr. J. A. Lavoie.
Actually the question of whether or not Mr. Lavoie can work his claims is one for the Department of National Defence to settle, and my department will again take the matter up with national defence to see if arrangements can be made which will enable Mr. Lavoie to develop his claims without interference with the R.C.A.F. installations.
I understand that my real estate officers have informed you that Mr. Lavoie's claim is very similar to the one filed by the Sullivan-Bourlamaque Gold Mines Limited as a result of the establishment of an airport at Val d'Or and that it was understood that you had agreed that negotiations could be held in abeyance, until a judgment is rendered in this case. Unfortunately, although some of the evidence has been heard the date of the final hearing is indefinite, and it may be some time before a judgment is rendered. I am afraid, therefore, that if the Department of National Defence feel that development of the claims cannot be allowed we will have no alternative but to await the completion of the Sullivan-Bourlamaque case.
I will write you further as soon as we have something definite from the Department of National Defence.
This letter is dated December 11, 1957.

Mr. Chairman, that letter was written in 1957 by the minister of transport of Canada Mr. Hees. Since then, Mr. Lavoie went on writing and communicating with the Department of National Defence; and again he was sent from post to pillar, trying to find out whether he was the owner of those claims or not, and whether the Department of National Defence could, without any compensation, expropriate land duly registered as claims with the provincial department in Quebec.
Here are the facts:
Mr. Lavoie has been since 1950 the owner of those mining claims, located on the present site of the Senneterre radar, whereas the building of that radar station only was started in 1951. When construction begun, Mr. Lavoie was formally denied entrance to the site of his claims when he wanted to work.
In 1958, the Department of Transport authorized him to proceed with his work within certain limits, and under entirely impractical conditions. Actually, Mr. Lavoie was refused the right to enter his own property.
By 1958, Mr. Lavoie had spent $51,113 with regard to these claims. At that time, the department concerned still refused to award Mr. Lavoie any damages, under the pretext that a similar case was pending in the exchequer court for the exact site occupied by the Val d'Or airport. That property had been taken over without any compensation being offered.
Therefore, I am asking the Minister of National Defence who could cut down the

Supply-National Defence expenditures in his department by $74 million, if he is now in a position to honour his commitment concerning Mr. Lavoie, in Senneterre, where the radar station is located, or if he intends to open negotiations in order to settle this matter which has remained unsolved for years.
Under the previous regime, Mr. Lavoie was already making trips from Val d'Or to Ottawa to meet the then member for Chapleau, Mr. Martel, the minister of mines and technical surveys and the deputy minister of national defence. The case was never settled under the Conservative regime and the present government does not seem willing to settle it either. I continue:
On November 10, 1960, judgment was rendered concerning the Val d'Or airport and Sullivan Gold Mines, Bourlamaque.
Until November 1961, the authorities had never claimed they had acquired from the province a right to the piece of land in question. On November 1, 1961, the Department of National Defence, in a letter signed by Mr. David McBrown, executive assistant, admitted that, to that date, the land concerned had not been transferred from the provincial to the federal government.
That was in 1961.
A few days after that letter was received, the deputy minister of national defence informed Mr. Claude R. Baillargeon, of Val d'Or, Mr. Lavoie's attorney, that he was ready to meet him to discuss the matter. As a matter of fact, the meeting took place on December 14 and 15, 1961. The compensation suggested then would not have been sufficient to cover the expenses incurred up until that time by Mr. Lavoie in legal fees, engineering fees and others to regain his rights.
On January 4, 1962, Mr. Lavoie indicated in writing the necessary conditions for his operations.
On May 25, 1962, the department of defence proposed a new method of operation under conditions impossible to comply with.
It would be superfluous to mention to you the extremely heavy correspondence at the office of Mr. Baillargeon, at the department concerned and at the department of lands and forests of Quebec about the matter.
The main point at stake now is not the amount of damages, since practically no serious proposal has been made concerning that matter, but the possibility for Mr. Lavoie to develop the mineral resources which he owns.
A fact worthy of notice is that three settlers have received compensation as early as September 1951, when their land or part of their land was transferred to national defence.
Must we therefore conclude that the department in question claims absolute priority without having to compensate the owners of mining claims? In fact, can the Queen in

right of Canada take over a property which was obtained legally from the Queen in right of the province? Perhaps the hypothesis may seem far fetched but facts prove that such an incident can and did happen.
The only way that argument could make any sense, would be to establish that the Department of National Defence had legal title before Mr. Lavoie. Otherwise, the department could offer Mr. Lavoie fair and reasonable compensation.
The last alternative has failed to materialize; as for the first one, official documents of the Quebec department of lands and forests prove the contrary.
A letter sent by the assistant deputy minister of lands and forests on October 15, 1957, bears witness to the fact that there has been no legal transfer yet. A letter dated November 1, 1961, and signed by the executive assistant to the Minister of National Defence reads partly as follows: "We are not yet in a position to give you a complete report, but we are informed that departmental officials are now ready to negotiate with Mr. Lavoie the settlement of his claim as soon as it appears that the Senneterre property was transferred to the department by the provincial department. The necessary steps have been taken to have the transfer made but the proper order has not yet been issued."
Even to this date, it is doubtful that the federal government has acquired legal title to that land where the radar station is located in Senneterre. I wonder if it is right for the government to act that way towards a Canadian citizen. Even if there is only one person involved and regardless of where the situation may arise in Canada, I feel that the Department of National Defence does not have the right to treat a Canadian citizen like that.
In the interest of the government, of human rights and of private property in Canada, I would therefore ask the Minister of National Defence to have the numerous cases like that of Mr. Lavoie settled in the nearest possible future.
Mr. Chairman, as I said a while ago, the Department of National Defence accounts for 25 per cent of the federal budget and its expenditures must be closely scrutinized. I agree that the Minister of National Defence is very competent and that he is an honest man-

Mr. Chairman, although I will now speak on the national defence estimates for the fiscal year 1963-64, I do not intend to prolong this debate but rather to bring my humble contribution to that delicate and very important matter which is the defence of our country. As the member from a constituency which along with the Gaspe riding gave to the Canadian armed forces during the last world war 35,000 men and women, many of whom fell on the battlefield, I feel doubly justified to speak.
Kindly allow me, Mr. Chairman, to express my most sincere gratitude and my great admiration to those courageous Canadians for the sacrifices they made in the name of a principle which is dear to us all: liberty.
To speak of defence is to speak of protecting our country against any eventual aggressor. When I say "our country", I mean its human capital as well as its territory. It is to speak of protecting our most cherished rights, our tongue, our faith, our traditions. It is, in short, to speak of safeguarding our democracy and our liberties.
In this framework, I feel that defence must be put above partisanship, because it is impossible for any country to have a true defence policy if it is bound by petty and often selfish interests that might be dictated by such and such a political party. Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I intend to remove all traces of partisanship from these few remarks.
I wish to devote the few minutes allotted to me to speak very briefly about the necessity of a good defence system for Canada and its responsibilities as a member of NATO and I will conclude with a few general comments.
In the first place, we, Canadians, should thank divine Providence for having spared our country from the disasters of war which the European countries and other continents have known for centuries. However, with the progress of science, with its effects in the military field as well as in all the others, with the development of the atomic bomb, jets, intercontinental missiles, etc. the enemy is at our doors. And we know some dictators who, if they would now decide to conquer the world, would represent a greater threat to Canada than the danger which existed 15 or 20 years ago.
Faced with such a prospect, no country, including Canada, can afford to disregard its
Supply-National Defence own means of defence. When one thinks that only one mistake, wherever it might be made, can soon degenerate into a world-wide disaster, there should be no hesitation about the necessity for our country to be ready for any emergency in order to protect its own territory. Therefore, I feel that Canada should have an army, an air force and a navy equipped with the most modern and efficient weapons. I will be told that all this would cost huge amounts of money that a country like ours, large in size but rather small in population, cannot afford. To that I reply that in order to protect itself, any country must be willing to make the necessary sacrifices if it is to survive.
To come back to what I was saying at the outset of my remarks, no price is too high to preserve one's freedom and the control over one's territory. After talking with our French, German or British friends who suffered from the disastrous effects of the numerous wars they experienced, it is realized what sacrifices those people made and are still ready to make and the price they are willing to pay in order to protect their freedom and to banish the curse of war which, according to the present outlook, would be a nuclear war.
It would be an overstatement perhaps to suggest that Canada, with its existing possibilities, could eventually hope to beat off alone an attack launched against its territory. That is why it must necessarily rely on the co-operation of its partners, the closest and the most powerful being the United States. This brings me to the second part of my statement, namely the North Atlantic treaty.
Shortly after the second world war, western democracies expected that a new era would begin an era of security. Demobilization was quickly undertaken as our faith was then put in the U.N. However, the Soviet policy very quickly cast a gloom over this fine dream. Before this sad prospect of Russia which had already annexed several countries, namely Poland, Finland, Czechoslovakia, etc. and wished to extend its rule throughout the world and in view of the inefficiency of the U.N. as a result of the repeated vetoes of Russia, there remained only one possibility for western countries to ensure their security: to unite in order to protect themselves.
Such was the origin of the North Atlantic treaty which was signed on April 4, 1949. This treaty states that the member countries are:
-determined to safeguard the liberty of their people, their common heritage and their civilization established on democratic principles, individual freedom and the rule of law.
Canada was one of the first 12 countries to sign that treaty. On that score, our
