Supply-National Defence country, as long as that multilateral agreement lasts, must have the best means of defence which will allow it to take the action that it will deem necessary, in case of any aggression against one or several of the contracting parties to the treaty.
Knowing, at least fairly well, the military might of the Soviet union, and its determination to achieve first place in the field of nuclear energy, and its admitted intention to spread all over the earth its communistic philosophy, by all the means available to it, the NATO members, and Canada among them, cannot afford to neglect looking after their defence, if they want to save the threatened democracy. It is useless to say, in the present context, as long as there is no ban on nuclear arms, that any possible world war would not lead to the use of the atomic bomb. Consequently, if the North Atlantic treaty has any meaning, the signers should be ready to face their obligations by being provided with the best defensive weapons.
However, considering the mutual fear of complete destruction, considering the terrible consequences of an atomic war, it is unlikely, though not impossible, that we will have eventually to suffer the atrocities of such a war. In view of these developments, the members of NATO will be called upon to change their defence policy.
According to information available, our powerful neighbours, the United States, are reputed to have enough nuclear arms to face an atomic war with Russia. If we can realize the rapidity and the destruction capacity of the nuclear weapons which these two countries have, I am of the opinion that it is useless to carry on the making of such a costly weapon which burdens the budget of all the countries involved, since it seems likely that the American reserves are adequate to meet any possible aggression.
This does not mean, however, that Canada, a member of NATO, should discontinue its defence program and cut all its expenses in this field. However, our country must increase its endeavours to equip its three services with the best conventional defence weapons, which are considered as most effective and least expensive, and not hesitate to discard equipment, material and armament which are obsolete or not effective enough.
The progress of science is so fast nowadays that a more serious study of each weapon likely to meet modern military requirements should be made in order to avoid finding ourselves in a situation at least uncertain, with an obsolete equipment, even before it is used.
I also suggest that the Department of National Defence should not be used to settle
[Mr. Bechard.l

the problem of unemployment in this country. Through a carefully conceived economic planning and a genuine Canadian defence policy, in compliance with our commitments in NATO, we would avoid these lay-offs which never fail to happen after the slightest change in our defence policy.
Before I conclude my remarks, I would like to express the hope that our country, which has always co-operated with its allies in order to establish a genuine and lasting peace in the world, will continue, together with the other western powers, to turn its endeavours toward that ultimate goal, without however yielding to ingeniousness and neglecting its own protection against an artful aggressor whose greatest wish, let us not forget it, is still to spread its totalitarian tenet to the whole world.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Definitely, if it is a relevant one.
Is the hon. member in favour of Canada being equipped with American nuclear warheads?

I should like to thank the minister for the kindly references he made to myself and to my predecessor in office, the Hon. George Pearkes, at the beginning of his remarks. I appreciate what he said and I know General Pearkes will appreciate it, also.
Before going into the subject matter of the debate I should like to make one comment on the statement by the hon. member for Vancouver East to the effect that there was no defence policy while the Conservatives were in power. On the contrary, we had a very definite defence policy. I stated it in the most explicit terms in presenting the estimates of the department to the House of Commons in September, 1961, which was the first opportunity I had of making such a statement. I expressed it, also, in dozens of speeches across the country. I know the hon. member for Vancouver East is a fair-minded man, so I should just like to ask him to turn up in Hansard the speech I made on September 11, I think it was, 1961, when I made a definite statement on defence policy. I should like him to read that statement and then come to his own conclusions. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, there were definite statements of policy made in white papers and blue papers throughout the period when the Conservative government was in power.
I turn, now, to the remarks made by the minister and to the particular matters under

discussion. To begin with, I must say I was shocked and disappointed by the statement which the Minister of National Defence made to the committee this afternoon. I had expected much more and much better. First of all, I think his statement gave the impression that a program of scrapping right and left was in progress without either a policy or a plan-that is, if we are to accept the statement that the government's review of policy has not yet been completed and that no definite decisions will be reached with regard to these matters until the recommendations of the defence committee have been studied. This is the situation presented to us, and it would appear to be correct. However, I submit that the government cannot have it both ways. Either the reductions announced must relate to a policy, or they make no sense at all. For this reason I think the government is on the horns of a dilemma in this connection. If the reductions announced in the hon. minister's statement are related to a definite defence policy, then the minister has refused to disclose to the house what the policy and the plans are to be. If that is the case, I think we have reached a point at which parliamentary government is not operating properly, and both the minister and the government could not be too strongly condemned for their part in such a situation.
On the other hand, if we accept the general tenor of the statement made, which conveys the impression that the reductions are nothing more than an unplanned, apparently desperate effort to cut defence spending by x million dollars, then I think the government is following an irresponsible and dangerous course. I think the situation should be resolved by a statement on the part of the minister because, otherwise, the committee is in an almost impossible position when it comes to considering these defence matters.
To deal with the actual statement which the minister made, may I say I think the inevitable effect of the long list of reductions which he announced, together with the cancellation of the frigate program and other reductions, will be to reduce the strength and effectiveness of our armed forces-it could not possibly have any other effect-and thus to reduce the contribution which we could make and which we are obligated to make to the joint defence of the western world under NATO and NORAD. I think, too, it will probably reduce our ability to meet any request which might be made of us by the United Nations in connection with its military interventions. In addition, these announcements are bound, in my view, to shake the confidence of our allies in our will and ability to meet the obligations we have assumed. Thus they will weaken our position in the
Supply-National Defence councils of NATO and in the councils of the world generally, and destroy, to some extent at least, our ability to influence decisions in directions we think they should take. This might well be the most dangerous result of widespread reductions such as have been announced, as far as I can gather without consultation with our allies and without there being any plan for replacement or for keeping up the general level of our contribution either to NATO or to NORAD, or to the service of the United Nations, whenever that might be required. At the same time, as far as our own forces are concerned, these announcements will deal an extremely heavy blow to the morale of all our armed forces and particularly to the morale of our reserve forces, and their ability to operate in any effective manner whatever.
I was disappointed that in his remarks the minister gave no indication when the implementation of the announced program to supply nuclear ammunition to the four weapons systems we have secured and which require it in order to be effective would take place. When the minister first assumed office I recall he made a statement that this would be looked after within a month. I have been extremely puzzled why there has been such a long delay in implementing the nuclear policy which I firmly believe in, the policy which I promoted when I was minister of national defence and which I was delighted to see the present administration take over. But I have been extremely puzzled why it has taken the present government so long to implement that policy. The government has given every evidence of dragging its feet in regard to this most important matter.
I think this chamber must and should have a statement from the minister telling us what the reasons for the delay are, and when the program will be implemented. I think we have been kept far too long in the dark in regard to this very important matter. As pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre this afternoon, until nuclear ammunition for these four weapons systems is supplied our present defence posture is much weaker and much poorer than at any other period in the past since the second world war, certainly since the Korean war, because of the fact that the effective armament we had then, the interceptor planes and so on, have been phased out and have disappeared while the more effective equipment which was planned to take their place has not yet been brought into operation. Therefore at the present time we are in a bit of a hiatus in that we have got rid of the armament we had, but we have not yet got new armament to take its place. In my opinion this situation constitutes a dereliction

Supply-National Defence as far as our obligations to our allies are concerned and as far as our obligations to the country are concerned in maintaining the security of this nation.
I do not have time tonight to comment on all the reductions announced by the minister, nor has there been time to study and assess them and thus come to some conclusion as to what the result will be. However, I should like to say a few words about some of these matters. The first one I should like to deal with is the cancellation of the general purpose frigate program, which was announced some time ago. I think this is an example of welshing on our naval commitments and our naval obligations as far as NATO is concerned. It amounts to a unilateral decision to reduce our naval contribution to NATO. I would be the last one to argue that the only naval program which is acceptable and which should be put into effect is the construction of the general purpose frigates. There are always alternatives in this regard. However, what I take the strongest possible objection to is the scrapping of a program decided upon after long study as being probably the best, looking ahead for the next 20 years and putting nothing in its place. If something had been put in its place I would say all right. People's ideas on these matters differ. We would at least be living up to obligations we have assumed, but to just scrap the program without having any replacement plan means that in effect we have taken a unilateral decision to reduce our naval contribution to NATO.
I asked the minister and the government a question whether a decision had been made to reduce our naval contribution to NATO and the answer was no, but the cancellation of the frigate program means that in effect that decision has been taken. Something is really being done here by indirection which I think the government perhaps dared not do openly and boldly. I think this is just as serious a dereliction with regard to our obligations and commitments as anything that could be instanced in respect of Canada or any other member of NATO.
I wonder whether the hon. member would answer a question on this point?
Yes.
When the hon. member was minister of national defence did he make any commitment to NATO for the building of these general purpose frigates?

Mr. Chairman, I did not make any specific commitment in regard to the building of the general purpose frigates. The point is that many years before we had agreed to supply a certain number of ships
[Mr. Harkness.!
to NATO. I do not say for a minute that our commitment should not be negotiated down or up. As a matter of fact, I would think most of the members of NATO would perhaps be insistent that it should be negotiated up rather than down. But as long as we are in that situation I think this cancellation is a very bad piece of business and causes a loss of confidence on the part of our NATO allies if, simply by allowing obsolescence to reduce the effectiveness of our NATO contribution, we thereby reduce the effort we are making on behalf of the alliance as a whole.
But you had no commitment?

Mr. Chairman, there is no use dealing in semantics with regard to whether you have a commitment or have not, whether you have a written contract or whether you have not. In NATO these things are arrived at as a result of long periods of conferences involving the permanent NATO council and at the NATO ministerial meetings. In many cases it is a matter of an agreement or a commitment by word of mouth being made at a NATO ministerial meeting. To try to pin this thing down to a matter of a written contract completely ignores what the realities of the situation happen to be.
To return to some of the particular matters that the minister mentioned, I must say that the termination of the Bobcat program fills me with a great deal of sadness. I do not for a moment absolve myself from all responsibility in connection with the failure of this program. As the minister said, it was started in 1954. We were the first nation really to get into the field of an armoured personnel carrier, and we should have been able to carry the program through and produce a carrier before anybody else. Instead we have had a long series of delays. To me the whole thing has been completely inexplicable and extremely frustrating. It was one of the most frustrating things I dealt with during the time I was minister, and I am still at a loss to understand why we failed in the way we did to carry this program through to completion.
It may well be, as the minister stated, that since the program has been so long delayed and as there is no possibility of anybody else buying the equipment with the result that the cost would be twice that for which we could buy somewhat similar equipment from somebody else, the wisest thing to do is to cancel the program. But I must say that when we embark on programs of this sort in the future I think there will have to be time limits placed on the commercial companies carrying on the work, and if the time-tables are not met, then that is the time to cancel the program, not years later after a great deal of money has been spent on it. In other words,

we have got to be much tougher in connection with development programs of this kind. Otherwise we are not going to get any place with them, and at the same time they are going to cost us a good deal of money.
There is quite a considerable list of reductions as far as the navy is concerned in the various reductions announced by the minister. With regard to the 10 auxiliary vessels which are going to be retired, all I can say is I do not know what vessels they are. Nobody else in this chamber, except perhaps the minister and associate minister, knows what they are. We are not, therefore, in a good position to say what the effect of this move will be.
Then, there is the reduction in the air squadrons. If you are going to continue to have an air arm in the navy, I think this is an error. If you are going to wipe out the air arm of the navy altogether, then the move may be justified. However, the mere reduction of the air squadron as a means of saving a few hundred thousand dollars, unless there is a definite plan behind it, is not defensible in my opinion.
I understand the Kamloops ammunition depot is to be closed. I think there are other members who will have something to say about that. However, there has been a lot of money spent on this depot-this applies to a lot of these other installations that are being closed-and it was put there for a definite purpose. I feel that pretty good reasons have to be produced for closing these various installations before it is possible for the members of this committee to accept their closing in this way. The same thing applies to Lon-gueuil, to the repair facilities at Sydney, to the installation in Newfoundland, and so on. Until we have had an opportunity to find out definitely what is being done, and particularly until the minister produces reasons which are acceptable for the closing of these installations, we have to look at this process with a very hard eye indeed.
Now, we come to the army. The turning of the northwest highway system to public works is something with which I would thoroughly agree. I must say that I attempted to do that during the time I was minister of defence. I did not believe it was a commitment the army should continue any longer. In fact, we probably should have given up some time ago. However, this brings up a question with which I think the committee ought to concern itself, and that is how much of the $40 million or $50 million of savings, which the minister is alleging in these reductions, are going to be actual savings and how much are merely transfers to some other department. I think a close examination will reveal that there is a great deal of what is represented as savings
Supply-National Defence which are not really savings at all but merely transfers to some other department.
In addition to the northwest highway system, there were certain airports and other installations which were being turned over for operation to another department. Then, there was the closing of Fort Churchill. So far as the army and R.C.A.F. are concerned, this appears to me to herald the end of cold weather training and research. I regret this move from that point of view. I think we have made a very distinct contribution to the entire NATO alliance by maintaining the facilities at Fort Churchill, particularly for research under cold weather conditions, and to determine what military personnel and equipment can do under these cold weather conditions. I feel that the closing of this installation is probably a very shortsighted policy in view of the great amount that is still to be learned, and needs to be learned, so far as operating under extremely cold weather conditions is concerned. This action is something which I believe needs a very good explanation before it can be accepted by this committee.
Now, I see that my time is getting rather short so I will go over some of the other matters rather quickly. I should like to protest particularly the closing of the repair depot at Calgary and also the closing of the auxiliary squadron there. This action will remove the R.C.A.F. entirely from a city which has been one of the great supports of the R.C.A.F. before the war, during the war and following the war. I can say nothing more than that I think it is a serious error and I protest against it. Once more, I should like to see reasons produced for this action.
I believe that the most serious criticism that can be made of the reductions the minister has announced relates to the reduction in the reserve force. So far as I can see, these reductions are designed to cut the reserve force by about 50 per cent. This is going to destroy this force which throughout our history has been the basis for our military build-up in time of emergency. I completely fail to understand the reason for destroying the reserve force in this country. I think there is no question but that this move indicates a definite change in policy, and I think the minister should announce that this is the case.
The cutting down of the army reserve to a maximum of 30,000 men, which I understand is the objective, means that the policy of using the reserve force for survival operations has to a large extent been thrown out the window. In other words, the whole emergency measures organization set-up, on which a large amount of money has been spent, has been

Supply-National Defence abandoned. This must be the policy or otherwise there would not have been such a serious reduction so far as the militia is concerned. As I have said, throughout our history, our military build-up has always been dependant upon the militia. So far as the immediate defence of Canada is concerned, the existence of a militia reserve is essential in order to get a sufficient number of men and units who are trained or semi-trained in the event of an attack on this continent. This is particularly true in the event that there should be a nuclear attack on this continent and there is a need for survival operations. Instead of reducing the number of the militia, the minister should be increasing the number.
I take particular objection to the reduction in the reserve force because during the time I was minister I made every effort possible to build up the morale, the spirit and the strength of the reserve force. I believe we had considerable success in that regard. I think there is no question about it, the comparatively small amount of money spent on the reserve force in comparison with the total military budget, is the best value we get for our defence dollar. I suggest to the minister that in cutting the reserve force to such a serious extent he has begun to make cuts, in an attempt to cut down defence expenditures, in the very worst way he could possibly have gone about it. I believe the minister said a total of about $5,250,000 would be saved in this way so far as the naval and R.C.A.F. reserve forces are concerned. I would estimate that about $5 million to $10 million would be saved by the reduction in the army reserve force. In comparison with the total budget of $1,500 million, that is a comparatively small amount and it destroys morale to such an extent, not only in the reserve force but in all the military forces, that it cuts down the ability to recruit and to build up rapidly in the face of emergency. I believe this is a completely unacceptable method of cutting defence expenditures. I plead most earnestly with the minister and with the government to wipe out this part of the program and to maintain the reserve forces, at least at the level that they have been during the past several years.
As the debate progresses I expect there will be a number of other matters on which I will wish to make comments, but at this particular time in closing I would like to point out that I have not dealt with general policy. However, if the debate develops along that line I should certainly like to present my views in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, I am one of the newcomers to this house. Up until just recently

I spent my life as a sailor in the Royal Canadian Navy, and let me say before anybody else gets a chance to say it, I am still at sea with regard to many of the activities that go on here.
This is the first time I have spoken in this chamber but I have served on a number of committees, and I know you will understand me when I say that, for me, the most interesting one is the defence committee. I should like to talk about this for a moment and, if you would permit me, I would like to take a short while to reminisce. I served as a very young man on a ship, the H.M.S. Hunter, a destroyer in the British Mediterranean fleet. For some 23 years now she has been lying at the bottom of Narvik fiord with most of my former shipmates.
We had a motto in that ship which somehow captured our imaginations and united us as one body. I often remember it. It was "To strive, to seek, to find and not to yield." In my opinion this would be suitable in many ways as a motto for the defence committee, so many members of which I see in the house tonight. So many of us are veterans that I feel we are drawn together by our common experience, and to me there is a very obvious wish to set aside many of the differences that plague us in this house and to get on with the job that a defence committee is supposed to do-to get on with the job that has to be done. We all know that we are facing a most difficult problem, and I think we are generally striving and seeking for the answer.
My riding of Victoria, which contains both a permanent army garrison and the Esquimalt navy base, has long and close military connections. We do most of the shipbuilding on the west coast, and altogether I suppose there is no town in Canada as affected as we are by shifts of defence policy. Not only are the servicemen affected, but our shipyards employ some 4,000 men, and their wages are a major factor in our economy. I must admit that the recent decision to purchase three submarines in Great Britain, which came as it did on the heels of the cancellation of the frigate program, came as an unexpected blow to me and to the people of my riding.
Victoria is going through an anxious time while the government decides what course it is going to take in defence, but the restraint which the people and the press of Victoria have shown so far demonstrates their understanding of the situation and I as their member appreciate this more than I can say. But I cannot stress too strongly that once a decision on defence policy has been made, some speedy and imaginative action on the part of the government will be necessary to

pump new life into the defence industries in Victoria and elsewhere, if they are to be kept alive.
Coming back to the defence committee, Mr. Chairman, I get the feeling that perhaps too much may be expected from it. The developments of science and technology over the past 20 years have made so-called defence experts out of anyone who wants to voice an opinion, for the very understandable reason that there are just not any comprehensible rules of defence and war any more. One is dealing these days with speeds of thousands and tens of thousands of miles an hour, and with hundreds of millions of tons of explosive power, and these are almost beyond ordinary human comprehension.
The point I am getting at is that we on the defence committee, and I certainly include myself, are not experts on military defence and we do not pretend to be. Through our travels and our briefings we can become well informed, but I think that is about as far as it can go, and it would be wrong to expect us to be specific and detailed in our advice or in our observations to the House of Commons. I would suggest that we have, however, a very useful role to play in pointing out some general signposts and some general guidelines for defence policy. I believe that is what we are trying to do.
The committee has not yet presented any report. I do not want to anticipate it, but I did want to point out that there are limitations to what the committee can rightly be expected to produce when it has built-in restrictions on the type of information it can acquire and when it has been in existence only such a short time.
I would like to support the suggestion of the hon. member for Fraser Valley that consideration be given to making this a permanent committee of the house, and now I am going to leave that subject because my time is limited.
It may interest some hon. members to know that in recent months I have been twice to Europe with the NATO parliamentarians, and while over there I was fortunate in being one of those who were able to travel from the northernmost tip of Norway to as far south as Turkey, which is the southernmost hinge of NATO. I also visited our Canadian army brigade and R.C.A.F. wing in France and Germany.
As a navy man I naturally went prepared to be critical, but I agree in all sincerity with the remarks the minister has made. We have every reason to be proud of our servicemen. All over Europe, from every quarter, we were complimented on them. They are held in the highest regard by the military and by civilians alike, and we were gratified, but
Supply-National Defence not overly surprised, to hear that their contribution to European defence far outweighs their numbers. I particularly noted how high their morale was. They are giving a good account of themselves and, while this is not news, I want to pay a tribute to them in this house.
While our Canadian forces are playing an important part in Europe, I must confess that in recent times I have felt that perhaps we should be paying greater attention than we have to defence on and around this continent, where I believe we have an even bigger role to play in the future. There is no doubt in my mind, and I think it is generally agreed, that it is what I call, for want of a better term, the weapon and defence equilibrium between the east and the west which provides us with our peace today, and which will continue to do so until some better arrangements can be made.
Today the heart of western defence is on this continent. Where do the nations of Europe look when the chips are down? If this is the case, then it is of vital importance to us all that this equilibrium be maintained at all costs and that our western side of the balance, particularly that major portion of it which lies on this continent, be given special care and attention.
I do not think there is much argument that the two main threats to both the east and the west are the other sides intercontinental ballistic missiles and missile carrying submarines. Against neither of these at the moment does there appear to be a satisfactory defence. But I am convinced, by the evidence of history and by the information we have gathered in committee, that a defence against both of these will be developed some time in the future. Enormous efforts are being put by both the east and the west into finding this solution. It will come, probably discovered by both sides at about the same time, and when it does the defence equilibrium must be quickly re-established. Because of our geographic position, next to the core of the western alliance, we Canadians will most assuredly have an important part to play, and if we are not prepared to take on the job, the United States or even NATO itself will demand the right to do it for us; and I cannot believe that Canadians would want that. I am making this point at some length, Mr. Chairman, because there is a not unnatural disposition on the part of all defence planners to discount forces for which there is no immediate urgency. I can understand this in view of the high costs involved; but security, we all know, is not cheap and efficient military forces, be they navy, army or air forces, just cannot be created or recreated overnight. They are the product

Supply-National Defence of years of training and experience, and if there is a foreseeable need for them in the future, we destroy or debilitate them at our peril.
I believe there is a need, a foreseeable need, for all our armed forces, but I am thinking of the navy particularly at this moment because they have come in for some pretty hard knocks lately and because dealing with half of the problem that I outlined, the missile-carrying submarine part, is their business. We have an admirable navy which is only now beginning to realize its full promise. Our Canadian navy has made a specialty of antisubmarine work-and it is good at it; make no mistake about that. If it is not capable at this moment of coping with fast nuclear powered submarines, I venture to say it is because this is a comparatively new threat and the R.C.N. has never been provided with a means of developing this capability. The threat is there; it is a threat that lies off our coasts perhaps today, and it is a major threat to the entire western alliance both now and increasingly in the future. I suggest that we will be shirking our responsibility if we do not busy ourselves right away with the task of preparing in earnest to meet this threat. I suggest this is no time to cut down the capability of our navy and I am glad to see there is nothing, to my mind, in the minister's statement today to indicate that the navy's capability is being permanently cut back. Bearing in mind the facts of the present and the probabilities of the future, we should in my view provide our navy with the type of naval vessels, equipment and research facilities which it will use, and use well, to meet and beat the threat. I do not think Canadians realize what outstanding men we have in the submarine, antisubmarine and research fields.
As I see it, as parliamentarians our duty to the nation in this regard is quite clear, and I for one have every confidence that this government will act in a responsible and satisfactory manner in facing up to the facts when early next year it reveals its defence plans for the future. I think, Mr. Chairman, we can all see the necessity for change now in the armed forces if we are to make progress in the future. There are some difficult days ahead for the minister, but the job has to be done and I am sure no hon. member of this house envies him the job. After all the talk and advice is over, it is the minister who has to make the decisions, particularly the hard ones. It is he who has to wring the last cent's worth of effectiveness out of the defence dollar, and he
[Mr. Groos.l
has my sympathy and support. We make no contribution to security if as a nation we go broke on defence.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, with reference to the minister's statement this afternoon, I am pleased that Royal Roads will continue as a service college but I am saddened to think that the naval reserve division in Victoria is to be disbanded. I am sure, however, that its past and present members, most of whom I knew so well, will agree to disbandment, if in its passing there will follow a real contribution to the future well-being of the naval service in Canada. The urgent requirement today, surely, is for military forces in being, ready to go at a moment's notice.
I think I am right in saying that the Victoria naval reserve division, now called H.M.C.S. Malahat, was the first to go on active service in world war I, and I have a feeling that we have not heard the last of it yet. This prompts me to end my remarks with a question to the minister, and it is this: Should the former members of the reserve division in Victoria organize themselves into some sort of supplementary reserve or association which would permit them to continue their contact with the naval service, would the minister consider allowing them to use some of the naval facilities now in Esquimalt, provided this can be done at no cost to the crown?

Mr. Chairman, as a member of the special committee on national defence, I would like to seize the opportunity afforded by the study of the credits of the Department of National Defence, in order to say a few words about these credits, and about the task of the special committee.
As the members of the committee already know, we have had the privilege of visiting a few European countries which are members of NATO. We saw on the spot the progress accomplished in the defence set-up of the European continent, and we studied the condition and the role of the military forces of the alliance.
Those who have occasion today to visit western Europe, cannot fail to be struck by the revival of countries which were terribly ravaged by the war of 1939-45. They are also able to ascertain that the Atlantic alliance has proved a success, in so far as it prevented western Europe from being drawn into the communist orbit.
I think that the alliance has inspired the fundamental policy of the European members of NATO, and that it should consequently be protected.

By shedding completely all spirit of partisanship, the members of the special committee on defence have become capable to praise on the one hand the success of the alliance, and on the other, the fruitful contribution that our forces in Europe allowed us to make.
Mr. Chairman, the members of the committee have also been impressed by the clear-cut policy of the majority of the European countries in NATO.
This, by contrast, throws sadly into light the lack of firm policies of our country, and more particularly of the present government, concerning our true role in matters of defence.
Mr. Chairman, it is possible of course not to be entirely in agreement with the aims, the policies and the objectives of some of our allies, but we cannot fail to see that they, at least, have a clear and well-defined program, and seem to know where they are going.
Let us look at the situation in France which is one of the main powers of NATO, and which, under the guidance of President de Gaulle, is following a policy of nuclear arms, which she calls her program of "independent deterrent".
There is no doubt that France is today a nuclear power and that, in a few months or at the most in a few years, she will have an independent nuclear deterrent, and will be able to drop nuclear heads on any enemy territory.
In the field of defence, most of the efforts of the French are aimed at this very definite objective. A few allied countries approve that attitude while others condemn it.
And if you go to Germany now, you will find there again a very definite defence policy aimed at the reunification of the German soil, the protection of Berlin against communist aggression, the defence of the German territory, that of West Germany. It favours also the creation of a European nuclear force under direct NATO control, and the German authorities leave no doubt that they intend to pursue that objective.
The members of the committee also went to Denmark and I am of the opinion that the primary aim of that short visit was to see the part that a small country could play within the alliance. With a population of only four or five million people, Denmark does not expect to play a major part within NATO. In view of the strategic importance of its geographical situation in Europe, the Danish government is totally opposed to any form of nuclear armament whether it be the storage of nuclear warheads on its soil or the equipment of the Danish forces with offensive nuclear weapons.
Supply-National Defence
The stand taken by the Danish government is very clear on that matter. It is opposed to all nuclear arms of any kind, as far as the Danish soil or the Danish armed forces may be involved.
And I remember, when a member of the committee asked one of the chiefs of staff what would happen in case of a sudden attack from an enemy nation, the answer was: in case of emergency or attack, do not fear, we will get our nuclear equipment early enough. But until war breaks out we will be unswerving in our determination to oppose any acquisition of nuclear arms for our country.
Mr. Chairman, I make these remarks to indicate that it is possible for some countries, whose interests may be quite divergent, to work out a defence policy consistent with their needs.
As far as our country is concerned unfortunately, I regret that we were not given by the Minister of National Defence a clear and specific statement on the Canadian defence policy.
The minister commented this afternoon on the military situation of Canada, but his remarks were a strange contrast with the things he did not mention.
For example, at a conference in Toronto, he stated-and he repeated the same thing here -that the military requirements of Canada were under study and the military situation was a subject of constant study by himself and his experts.
But he seems unable to derive from his studies the elements that must be selected to work out our defence policy.
As a matter of fact, the minister this afternoon has not given us any idea of the necessary steps to protect the Canadian territory and the rest of North American territory. He said nothing at all about that.
He did not talk either of the most effective part our military forces might play in NATO.
He also ignored a current topic, namely the integration of Canadian armed forces.
And he did not say a word of the future role of the Canadian navy, the air force, and research in military technology.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that instead of laughing during our remarks, the minister should rather listen to them. Since he is introducing his estimates for the first time, he should make an effort to give the committee members and the Canadian people an outline of the way public funds allocated to defence are spent.
The minister stated that 77 per cent of the estimates were for the maintenance of the Canadian armed forces, while only 16 per

Supply

National Defence cent are earmarked for designing and developing new weapons and for supplying our armed forces with the required equipment as well.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that something is rotten in the state of Denmark. It seems to me that too large sums are spent for the maintenance of the armed forces. In other words, it is much too expensive to train a soldier and to get him ready for action.
And although the estimates of the Department of National Defence account for 25 or 26 per cent of the national budget, I think Canada does not spend enough to keep up to date as regards military technology.
It is recognized today that defence is mostly ensured by technological facilities. Military technology develops constantly, and a country which does not devote the necessary amounts to research in military fields, economic fields and others, will certainly lose its rank among the progressive and industrial powers. And Canada, unfortunately, is in the process of so doing, in military fields as well as in others.
Mr. Chairman, I believe it is time the government revise entirely its attitude on defence and give a clear and unequivocal reply to the questions which the Canadian people ask themselves, and rightly so, as concerns their constantly threatened security, should no attention be paid to it.
Mr. Chairman, the committee members have also found other things in the course of their European tour.
For instance, it may be said the morale of the air division is excellent, that it has very well-disciplined troops. In fact, were they provided with the necessary equipment, they would be ready for combat. In brief, they are a credit to Canada.
There is nothing wrong with those troops. Our allies and the members of NATO all agree that the Canadian forces, whether they be the army or air forces, are first class troops in every respect.
But the minister has some problems to settle concerning the air division. He said a few days ago that a situation not very satisfactory existed, that is that half of the air division stationed in France did not have available the aircraft or the equipment required by those aircraft and so was prevented from playing the part which could be expected from it as a member of the NATO armed forces.
It is not enough for the minister to say that an unsound and regrettable situation exists. As a minister, he has the responsibility to settle that situation, and that, first of all, in the interest of the members of our air force, as well as in the interest of the defence of Canada and of the NATO nations.

But the minister gave no indication, neither in his speech the other day nor in his remarks this afternoon, of the steps he intends to take to settle that problem.
Now, as far as our land forces are concerned, no one can question the ability of those soldiers as fighting units. But those soldiers have not yet received the equipment they need to fully play their part and in fact-and the members of the committee had an opportunity to find that out-the equipment available to them more often than not is old, obsolete and in a conflict, could play neither a protection nor a defence role.
Mr. Chairman, that is an intolerable situation which the minister has the responsibility to settle without any delay.
There is also the matter of tactic nuclear weapons which are or would be available to the army and the forces joining that army in case of a conflict.
Mr. Chairman, the members of the committee were a little frightened by the unconstrained manner with which the members of the army use those nuclear weapons during training. In listening to some commanding officers reporting on the situation which would probably exist in case of real attack, you might have thought that those nuclear weapons can be used as any other conventional weapon, that if the enemy should attack in sufficient number, a division commanding officer would only have to give some order and the soldiers included in that division would immediately start using nuclear weapons. It seems to me another philosophy should exist about the hypothetical use of nuclear arms in case of war.
I know that the Minister of National Defence will say: that is impossible because nuclear arms cannot be used without the authorization of the highest authorities, possibly the President of the United States. It is no doubt true in theory but, in practice, the members of the committee got a very clear impression that the order to use those nuclear arms would come from the commanding officer at the brigade or expeditionary force level. Thus the danger of setting up nuclear bases and also the indescribable horror that would result from the start of a nuclear war. The danger is very real and it seems to me that our soldiers show an unconcern that almost shocks the observer with regard to the use and control of those nuclear arms. I would like the minister to give us some detailed information about that.
Personally, I feel that as far as the use of those tactical nuclear weapons is concerned, special units should be established which would be well trained to use those weapons in

case of war, would be aware of the consequences if they were used and would not use them unwisely in the confusion that an attack would create.
It seems to me that, in that regard, military leaders should get very definite orders from political leaders.
Mr. Chairman, we spend a great percentage of our total budget for military purposes. It seems to me that we should try very hard to reduce it, if possible, because a quarter of the total budget going for defence, that is too much. If Canada wants to play an influential part, it should direct its efforts towards the achievement of peace.
The other day, I heard about a project submitted by President de Gaulle to some of the main industrial countries: this project consisted essentially in an appeal to reduce military expenses by one half of one per cent and to use those savings for research on cancer.
I do not know whether Canada has received an invitation to join that group of countries, but I know that others were invited and reacted in a positive way. I have in mind the case of England, for instance, which immediately sent some of its military experts to Paris, as well as some specialists in the cancer field to study the possibilities.
Canada, which is a medium-sized power, should rather direct its efforts to attaining peace.
There seems to be some contradiction between the Minister of National Defence and one of his fellow members of the cabinet, that is, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), with regard to the creation of a mobile force operating under the United Nations.
Indeed, the Minister of National Defence admitted the other day that there did not seem to be much enthusiasm as far as a police force operating under the United Nations was concerned. This very morning, the Secretary of State for External Affairs very categorically stated that he favoured setting up such a force and that he believed Canada could play a useful part in that field. He favoured the immediate setting up of a Canadian force which would be available to the United Nations on request in any situation which would be considered a menace to peace.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is through such actions that Canada, as a medium-sized power, with rather limited financial resources, will be able to play a useful part. It has often been said that this country is highly respected by all the others and more particularly by the important blocs within the United Nations. A great many of those new countries look to Canada playing a constructive role.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if we want to play a constructive part on the world stage, we
Supply-National Defence should first be in a position to define our objectives, and no other than the minister and the government can do so, and wisely shape our policy.
I therefore ask the minister, before the discussion of his estimates is over, to give the members of this committee a full and unambiguous statement on the part to be played by this country in respect of defence, and to prove that the amounts asked for will be spent to good purpose, for attaining the true objective of this country, which is a durable peace.

Mr. Chairman, defence is a subject that is currently attracting widespread attention across Canada, and well it might. Defence expenditures consume approximately $1.6 billion annually. This is over 7 per cent of our gross national product. It is nearly one quarter of our national budget. It represents about $90 for every man, woman and child each year in this country.
It is obvious that expenditures of this order have a profound economic effect on our country. But defence is more than just plain economics. Defence is our only protection for our way of life. Defence is a factor that influences our relationships with all countries of the world, both east and west. Our activities in this field affect our strength when we bargain with other countries politically and economically.
Because of the importance of the subject I am particularly glad that the government, parliament and Canadians generally are taking an increasing interest in the problem. I particularly welcome the establishment of the special committee on defence that has been set up to study some of these topics. I think that already, through press coverage of some of our meetings, there is a greater awareness among Canadians generally of some of these problems. Not only is there greater awareness but I think there is probably also greater discussion of these problems. To me the increased interest and discussion are in themselves a pretty worthwhile result.
To deal in any depth with the problems of defence, Mr. Chairman, would require an outline of the threat that is posed against us, the strategy that has been devised to meet that threat, the alliances that have been formed to carry out this strategy and, finally, the part that we might play within these alliances. None of these topics is simple and, as we know, there are widely differing views on many of these things, particularly among some of the nations of NATO.

Supply-National Defence
Some speakers have already given some background information in this area. I believe that at this stage this is as far as we should go. I think that we of the defence committee must first get together as a committee, hammer out our views and prepare our report. I think that a general debate before we do this would not be wise. In my view the report must cover all those topics having to do with strategy, alliances, Canada's part and many other aspects if it is going to be of any benefit.
The minister has promised to issue a white paper on defence early in the next session covering government defence policy. I believe this white paper, plus the report of the defence committee should provide good material for a first class, informed debate on defence policy and I hope that debate takes place early in the next session. Because of this I am going to resist the temptation to expound at length on defence problems, and instead wait until that debate.
Today we are dealing with the defence department estimates and it is not my desire to delay unduly the passing of these estimates. I do have one point, however, that I think is important, and in view of the minister's statement today I believe it is particularly pertinent. My point is that I believe our defence expenditures should be for one purpose only, that of providing the maximum useful defence effort for each dollar spent. I do not think we should confuse defence dollars with social capital. It seems to me that an attempt to solve social problems with defence dollars produces a second rate defence effort and a second rate solution to some of our social problems.
During the last few months there has been discussion in the house concerning the cancellation of the frigate program, the Penhold air base, the base at Churchill and other matters. Undoubtedly as a result of the minister's statement today there is going to be a great deal of discussion about some of the items he mentioned.
Much of the discussion has disturbed me. I have been disturbed because some of those who argue against these changes in our defence program do not argue on the basis of the military necessity of these changes but argue on the basis of the social and economic effects of the changes. In effect their argument is: "You cannot reduce this item, you cannot reduce this program, you cannot cancel this base, not because the particular item is needed, but because the communities surrounding it cannot survive economically without it." This approach of applying social reasoning to military problems is wrong in my opinion. I should like to make it clear, Mr. 

Chairman, that I am not defending or discussing the military reasons for some of these decisions. It is possible some of them might have been wise and some of them might have been foolish. This is not the point at issue so far as I am concerned. What is at issue is the basis we use for judging these decisions.
Canada cannot afford to spend all it wants or all it should on defence; no nation can. It is, therefore, vital that each dollar we spend be spent to the best possible advantage. In my opinion, this means applying the sort of techniques that are now called military cost effectiveness studies. We cannot afford to acquire, maintain or keep in operation an airplane, a ship, a weapon or a base that serves no really useful military purpose.
The government must make military decisions and it must answer for those decisions. I believe that a government must also be aware of the social problems which are raised in making military decisions, and equally a government must answer for the steps it takes to meet these social problems. But a government should not avoid making a military decision in order to prevent facing a social problem.
I hope that in the future governments will not be taken to task for changes in defence expenditures because those changes are going to hurt some section of the country. I hope governments will be taken to task for making a decision that hurts some section of the country, and for not taking some steps to alleviate that hurt. A government should be taken to task also, obviously, for making a wrong military decision. We must accept this split between the military effects of a decision and the social problems it raises. I believe, as a matter of fundamental principle, that failure to do this is going to result in wasted defence dollars and it will result also, I believe, in poor economic conditions because, defence dollars are an inefficient way of providing social capital.
There is a second important reason for accepting this principle and accepting it now. I think all of us in this country, in fact everyone in the world, hopes that some day we will be able to move in the direction of finally achieving disarmament. This is going to have a disastrous disruptive effect on our economy if we have not prepared plans in advance. If we are going to work towards this goal, we have to start now in preparing for its realization. No one knows if it is ever going to be militarily possible to achieve disarmament, but if it is, and if the military situation will allow this, then let us not be in a position where we have to let social problems stand in the way of achieving this goal.

I think if we are going to prepare now to move in this direction, we must first think realistically about the role of our defence expenditures. We must accept the fact that defence spending is for military purposes only. We must learn also to adjust our economy to the change in military demands. We have to learn to use the tools, some of which already exist, such as the economic council, technical retraining and the area development agencies as well as the Department of Industry and other departments of government, to alleviate some of the social problems that are going to result from changes in military spending.
If we do not develop these skills, if we do not develop our thinking along lines which will enable us to accept the fact that our military spending is only for defence purposes, then in the future we are going to be unable to adjust ourselves to the acceptance of any possible decrease that might be militarily possible in the field of armaments. We are going to be unable to develop this thinking and those skills which we will have to develop to accept disarmament, if that ever were possible. In addition to that, if we do not adopt these techniques, if we do not adopt this type of thinking, we are going to continue a course which will waste our current defence dollars and which will, I believe, lead to incorrect solutions of some of our social problems.
In the future, Mr. Chairman, I hope to hear lots of debate, lots of argument and lots of criticism of the defence practices of this and future governments, because the subject is important enough to warrant this. I hope that these debates, these arguments, and these criticisms will be based on sound fundamental principles.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I wish to take this opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Minister of National Defence. At the outset, I should like to say that I am certainly not a defence expert, I do not profess to be one. In fact, I could fill a very large book with all I do not know about defence. However on behalf of my constituents, I should like to say a few words this evening with regard to the minister's statement. He said that the Point Edward naval base would be one of the establishments that would be closed. I was shocked and horrified, Mr. Chairman, by the minister's statement concerning the closure of this base. I wonder if he realizes the economic implications of this decision. The previous speaker dwelt for some time on the social problems connected with these decisions. He took the negative side, and I shall take the positive.
Supply-National Defence
I should like to point out how important this base is to the people of my area. There are between 500 and 600 employees at this base. I understand that when the minister is through with his cutbacks and closures we will probably have only 100 left there. I may be wrong, and perhaps we will have 200. However, what will happen to the other 300 or 400? As I understood the minister's statement, he said that the navy had maintained a naval repair facility at Point Edward naval base in Sydney. In fact, the minister does not even know where the base is. It is not in Sydney at all, but is at Point Edward in the municipality of Cape Breton. He then said that this repair facility would be discontinued, but the navy would continue to operate the stores depot and record centre at this location. According to the minister, it is not planned to have any of the reductions in ship repair work at the Point Edward naval base take place until after the beginning of the new fiscal year on April 1, 1964. He is being very kind in this instance: He is going to allow these employees to have Christmas dinner.
Then, he goes on to say that this will ensure that operations at the naval base are gradually to be reduced after that date in relation to the development of alternative opportunities for employment. I hope the minister will tell us what those alternative opportunities for employment are in the Cape Breton area. I just hope that he will spell them out when he replies.
There will be adjustments involved, according to the minister, for some of those now employed at this base. This is another typically vague Liberal statement. In order to assist, efforts will be made, as the minister has said, to organize training and retraining programs in co-operation with the provincial government, wherever these will be suitable. I know that Bob Stanfield, the premier of Nova Scotia, has done a tremendous job in trying to retrain people and help them. However, I do hope the minister will tell me, after these people are retrained, where they are going to find employment in Cape Breton.
The minister makes another very clear statement when he says that other measures will also be introduced as they appear appropriate in the circumstances. I should like him to tell us what those other measures are and how soon they will be introduced. How soon will he, and the Minister of Labour who is also from Cape Breton, arrange to get these people back to work.
I would like to give the committee an idea of how important this is economically, and in this instance I would like to quote. The department gave me a reply to a question on October 16 indicating that for the last year of the previous Liberal regime the payroll

Supply-National Defence at Point Edward base was $1,856,851. Last year, 1962, it was $2,634,767. The minister should realize what this is going to do to the economy. I suggest that when we came into power in 1957-58 the plan of the previous Liberal administration was to close this base at that time, but the government after 1958 kept the base going and, as I have indicated, the payrolls were increased. The continuance of this base was brought about through the efforts of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and of the very efficient government of that day. I regret to say we do not seem to have an efficient government now.
I am no expert on defence but I do hope I can get through to the minister how important and serious this is to the economy. On June 10 of this year I asked the minister:
What is the planned schedule of refits for Point Edward naval base for the next year?
The answer, which bears his initials P.T.H. on it said:
The refit plan for Point Edward naval base calls for the refit of one frigate or equivalent at any one time making an approximate work load of three frigates per year.
I wonder what has happened to that decision. When the previous administration was in power the navy arranged at that time for a proper schedule of refitting, but I do not know what has happened since.
Again on June 17 this year I asked the minister:
1.	What are the plans for the expansion of the magazine facilities at the Point Edward naval base?
2.	What plans has the government for the expansion of other facilities?
He replied:
1.	It is intended to expand the magazine facilities by constructing four ammunition storehouses, one ammunition laboratory, an access road and improvements to fencing in the magazine area.
2.	It is intended to provide bulk storage for ships' bunker fuel and aviation gas with receiving and dispensing lines.
They went ahead and called a contract. Tenders were submitted; but then they cancelled that tender and did not do anything about the second contract. Today, however, they really did something. They are going to knock everybody out of work-and this, along with all the other cutbacks since this government took over, cutbacks in five or six different departments. In fact there was a cutback in the constituency of the Minister of Labour the other day.
This is the pitiful administration which said, "The Liberals have the answer." What answer are they going to give to these men who will be unemployed, and some of them have ten, 15 and 20 years service? Will the minister tell them, "Take a stand for tomorrow"? How are these people going to stand


for tomorrow? They will not have any jobs, to be able to eat. They will not be able to lie down, far less stand.
I just cannot understand this. Then there is the Secretary of State, and I am sorry he is not present tonight. Speaking at Summer-side, Prince Edward Island on March 26, 1963, he said:
A Liberal government will do everything to give this part of Canada equality in income and employment with the rest of Canada.
Is this the way they are going to do it? Is this the way the Minister of Finance is going to do it with his cutbacks and his crazy budget? The Secretary of State, again speaking at Summerside on March 26, as reported in the Charlottetown Guardian on March 27 said this:
It is the Liberal policy to see that every able person willing to work will have the opportunity to earn a decent living.
This is the way they are doing it. They are just laying the men off without any consideration. Yes, they are going to keep them on for a few months until they recover from the shock and that is the end of it.
Speaking at Toronto on March 23, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 25, 1963, the Secretary of State said:
Canadians have to face three outstanding problems:
-getting work for all Canadians;
-maintaining security and peace in the world;
*-bringing about the unity of Canada with equality of citizenship for all.
Then he said:
The Liberal party has answers to all these problems.
This is the way the Liberal party gets work for Canadians. Again, speaking at Summer-side on March 26, as reported in the Charlottetown Guardian of March 27 he said:
The Liberal program offers the people of Canada work and income security in peace, equality and unity.
My, my, these are wonderful words. I wonder how wonderful these employees will think they are, these employees who are going to be given-let us put it frankly-a kick in the pants by the Minister of National Defence and this inept and arrogant government. Why, Paul on the road to Damascus eventually saw the light, but I doubt if this Paul we are dealing with now will ever see the light.
Let us look at some other words that have been written about some of these illustrious and distinguished members of the cabinet. In the Edmonton Journal of October 1 we find these:
Just what is a politicians' word worth? Judging by the sad performance by Mr. Hellyer, not very much.

Last week the Minister of Labour, who is one of my colleagues from Cape Breton, made a special trip to Cape Breton. He appeared on television, and in his Buddha-like manner he was very glad to try and take some of the kudos and credit for the establishment of a heavy water plant. I regret he is not in his seat tonight, but I suggest he should go down this week end and appear on television, and smilingly announce the closure of the Point Edward naval base. After all, it is only the right thing for him to do.
I would suggest that the minister of defence should go down too, but I doubt if he would be allowed to come back, or even to get across the causeway into Cape Breton island. During the last election the Liberal candidate who ran against me, and other members of his party, made many great, glorious, and as some people thought, honest promises. They were going to do wonderful things for the economy of the maritimes and Cape Breton island, but instead we have this dastardly crime perpetrated on the people of Cape Breton island.
I suggest that the Minister of National Defence is not alone responsible for what has happened today, and let me say to the Secretary of State and to the Minister of National Defence-you certainly have not heard the last of this episode yet. Let me say to the Prime Minister, and I wish he were here tonight, that I invite you, sir, with all your so-called bow-tie diplomacy and your bland little smile, to go to Cape Breton and explain in the most diplomatic manner you can the mess into which you have placed Cape Breton island and this country.
These are the people who tried to do their utmost to assassinate the character and the government of John Diefenbaker. So far as I am concerned, after so much has happened in the last few months, and with today's latest episode, I suggest that some of these persons who are prominent in the Liberal party are not even fit to polish the boots of John Diefenbaker.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to a number of so-called debates on defence over the last ten years in this chamber, and we do advance. I realized how quickly we are advancing when I was listening to the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, because apparently we have now abandoned the pretence that these vast sums of money we spend on so-called defence have anything to do with defence; we realize now they are primarily designed to provide jobs for the people of Canada, which may be-
You mean you didn't know that before?

No, I did not know that before. I knew that our Tory friends for five years made the pretence that they were spending the money to defend Canada, and I know that for 22 years before that our Liberal friends made the same pretence, and I know that the present Minister of National Defence is in a position to again start making the same pretence. But, as I say, we do advance, because the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria has come out of the bushes and now we know what is the purpose of defence expenditures.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria was never in the bushes.
I see.

Oh, on anything. In the bushes is quite a good place to be. If I am annoying the hon. member-
