speechtext: No, I am enjoying it.

That is fine. Then I will suggest this is the basis upon which we should discuss these estimates. I sympathize with the hon. member in his concern for his constituents, and I suggest to him that his arguments are almost the same as the arguments that used to be advanced in Great Britain for relieving the aristocracy of that country from heavy taxation, because if they were taxed heavily they would be unable to employ so many footmen and housemaids as they would employ if they had a larger income. Therefore the effect on the economy of Britain would be very bad. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria suggests that we should not reduce our expenditures in this regard and should employ as many footmen and as many housemaids as possible. He does not seem to realize that if we employ these people in more useful ways, perhaps Canada as a whole might benefit.
I, like the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, make no pretensions at being a military expert. I have always been rather suspicious of the estimates of military experts, ever since I lost two horses for the government of Canada. In fact, I was almost before my time. Since my time they have put horses on the payroll: I took two of them off. This was almost 50 years ago, here in Ottawa. This is unveiling part of Canada's history, in what I am about to reveal. On this occasion I was sent with a number of my comrades to bring a number of horses from outlying stations into Lansdowne park. We were all given one horse to ride and another to lead. We were riding them bareback, I might say. The pair of horses that I had were not very well suited in their gait, and the one I was riding was much faster than the one I was leading. For this reason I was dropped off in the middle of the road, in the middle of the night. They vanished in the darkness and I said, "Well, I presume this is the sort of thing for which one gets shot at dawn. I had better get back and face the music." I trudged back to Lansdowne park, and mercifully the sergeant was blind drunk. He would not have known whether I had arrived with two elephants or nothing at all. From that day to this I have never heard of the two horses that I lost. I may say that for months I was in fear and trembling that at any moment I might be summoned before the authorities to answer for the two horses I lost. Ever since

then I have been a little doubtful about military experts and their estimates of costs, because if one can lose two horses 50 years ago I presume that you can lose several squadrons of aircraft now, without causing any more ripple of dismay.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: But they turned up on the payroll 40 years later.

That may be, but I do not think these lived that long. I thought that I did a service to the Canadian economy and that some farmer in the Ottawa valley got a team of horses which he would not otherwise have had. He probably increased his production with the use of these horses instead of their being wasted on useless military exercises. Instead they were set to work producing food.
Our defence policies in this country are, of course, inextricably bound up with our general external affairs or foreign policy. That is understandable because although within three years we are going to be celebrating ostensibly the one hundredth anniversary of Canada as a nation, in actual fact I submit that Canada is really only 50 years old; that it was in the process of the first world war that we first began to have any realization of national identity; that that national identity was underlined some 20 odd years later in the second world war. Therefore it is quite natural that we should always be equating our sense of national identity with a military exercise of some sort.
That, I believe, may be the cause of some of our present diseases and troubles in Canada, that we have been unable to find a military role and have therefore begun to doubt the reality of our national identity. Because we have been trying to find a military role for years. We have been spending countless millions or billions of dollars on an attempt to find a role which does not exist. I say it does not exist because that is the opinion and the advice that has been given to us time and time again both by military and scientific experts, when they tell us there is quite literally no defence in war, that no matter what our vigorous and active young Minister of National Defence may try to do, even he is not going to be able to evolve a means of defence. This is an extremely difficult emotional concept for people to take. Always they think that if they look somewhere else they will find some way of defending us, that there must be some way. It is understandable, because this is the first time in the history of the human race that mankind has had to face the fact that there is no defence, that no matter what man does, no matter how much of his 28902-5-350J
Supply-National Defence treasure and wealth and people's lives he may expend, there is no defence. Because there is no defence, there is, therefore, no real military role. Because there is no military role there is, I think, no sense of national identity in Canada.
I believe the search for this will-o'-the-wisp of a real military defence role is preventing us from really finding the worth-while role that Canada could be playing in the world today. With what tremendous fanfare of trumpets-perhaps that is not right because trumpets would not be wrapped up in quite so much wool-but with what eclat the Minister of National Defence announced the increase in Canada's aid program, to the staggering amount of about one tenth of the money we are spending on military expenditures. There is tremendous heart searching, and head scratching too, before any money is spent abroad, or at home, in developing the civilized aspects of our life. On the other hand, with what gay abandon we throw away a billion and three quarter dollars year after year, and year after year we have to admit to the fact that we get nothing for it if it were spent with the idea for providing defence for this country.
It may be that there is some sort of defence on the basis of the theory of the massive deferent, but if that is so we have played no part in it. I suggest that the speech of Mr. McNamara which my colleague from Vancouver East quoted today, and the speech of his subordinate Mr. Nietze some months ago, indicates quite clearly that if there is any validity in the theory of the massive deterrent it points quite clearly to the fact that the United States has everything which might deter any nation from now until doomsday.
However, I suggest there are other considerations to be taken into account too. History changes very rapidly. I note that, except for the lunatic fringe, practically every authoritative spokesman in the United States of America is now agreeing that we have moved into a new era. Someone remarked shortly after the tragic assassination of President Kennedy that there was one man who very few people seemed to realize had been placed in an extremely dangerous position because of this frightful event and that man was Nikita Khrushchev, who had risked his political life and neck-possibly more than his political neck-to reach a rapprochement with President Kennedy, and now had to do it all over again with the new President, attended by similar risks as in his attempts to reach a rapprochement with the late president. I think these considerations indicate that the situation for which the theory of the massive deterent was evolved no longer exists.

Supply-National Defence
I have repeatedly suggested in this chamber that only an assessment of the leaders of the Soviet union as criminal lunatics would lead anyone to suppose that they would launch an attack on North America, to create in North America a radioactive desert with the certainty that in their own territory a similar radioactive desert would be created. Why we have to go on pretending that the men in the Kremlin are half-witted or imbecile, or that their counterparts in the United States are half-witted or imbecile, is beyond my comprehension. I suggest it is because we are stuck in this absurd situation of trying to find something that does not exist, and that is a valid military role for Canada and a valid defence position for Canada, that we are unable to move into the new world which we might achieve.
I was perhaps rather rudely making fun of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria when I started my speech. He was concerned for his constituents, and I should like to extend that concern to another group we must consider, and that is the young men in our armed services. It is not good enough to advocate, and I for one would not for a moment advocate, that tomorrow morning we heave them all out of the service and put them on the labour market. However, I suggest that there is another role for them in the world today, a role which Canada should be seeking and achieving. That role is helping toward the development of the undeveloped areas of the world. We have in our armed forces a large number of extremely highly trained and intelligent young men whose services could be placed at the disposal of world development today. These young men could play a role in establishing a real foundation for global peace that they can never hope to give us by their present traditional role in a military defence force. I was very much struck with the quality of many of these young men when I was in Europe this autumn. They were young men of definitely extremely superior capabilities, young men who would not only be first class ambassadors for Canada but would also be the very type required to aid the newly-emerging countries in the development of their democratic institutions, their economic institutions, in the development of their whole society to take part in this twentieth century of the modern world. That is the sort of thing we should be doing, not harking back to a situation that is hopelessly banished forever; or perhaps not hopelessly; it is extremely hopeful that it has disappeared completely. I feel very strongly that it is because we are wasting our time, our efforts and our treasure in the pursuit of this will-o'-the-wisp, this foolish chase after 
something which does not exist, that we are allowing a friction to arise in this country which need not arise. If only we could place the economy of Canada at the service of this world development we might be able to forget that we are English Canadians or French Canadians or any other kind of Canadians except plain, ordinary Canadians. We might be able to go even further. We might forget we are Canadians and remember that we are human beings in a world which is daily getting smaller-a world in which the concepts on which defence policy is based today are largely outmoded.
I do hope that the government of Canada will eventually become courageous enough to make the sort of dramatic and useful gesture in the world which would advance the cause of peace much more effectively than the nonsensical expenditure on which we are now engaged, expenditure which gives rise to equally nonsensical debates in this house during which we hear supporters of the previous government denouncing the present government and supporters of the present government denouncing the previous government in turn, neither of the parties being prepared to face up to the real facts of life in a world in which there can be no defence in the military sense of the word.
I hope to live long enough to see the Minister of National Defence transformed so as to carry out a more useful function than his present one, able to apply his energies to the pursuit of peace, not to the pursuit of a nightmare by means which have completely lost their validity. Let us move into the 20th century, not back to a situation which no longer exists. It might be difficult for the minister to face such a concept, but I suggest that within a short time the role he is playing now will appear to him and to every other intelligent person to be as ridiculous as the roles played in the early stage of human history when every part of the earth was divided into warring states whose people fought with their neighbours. Today, we laugh at those people. We say they are primitive folk. Let us not be primitive in our own time. Let us realize that the revolutionaries of the laboratory have been at work, that the world has been reduced to a unit and that we must live together as human beings or be prepared to have no future generations to enjoy the world which could be built if we were to stop playing with our expensive and dangerous lead soldiers today.

Mr. Chairman, now that this dispute seems to be settled and the hon. members opposite are willing to let us state our views, I must say that I am pleased that we have, as elected members to this house with a fair majority, the right to voice our opinion, all the more as, since the setting up of the committee, I have attended all its meetings and followed its activities with an ever-increasing interest.
In my opinion, I am in a position, as well as any other member of this house, to make a worthwhile contribution to this debate.
Mr. Chairman, when considering the minister's estimates, we realize that this subject can give rise to many controversial discussions. Since this debate began, we saw some members take a rather radical stand against the decisions just announced by the Minister of National Defence.
As the previous speaker said, this enables us to realize to what extent our economy is based on a military organization.
In the course of my remarks, I would like to show to what extent the committee established by this house early in the session was in a position to play a useful part. It will be remembered that the establishment of such a committee was advocated by our group in previous election campaigns. We were very pleased to note that the present government saw fit to set it up as one of the first items of its program. The most satisfying feature was that members of the various parties who sit on the committee succeeded in keeping politics out of their deliberations. In my opinion, the committee's mandate was of such importance that political considerations had to be left out if it wanted the present government to act upon its recommendations.
I feel that the most serious question the committee had to examine was the advisability or importance of Canada's role as a middle power within NATO and in Europe especially.
During our discussions and also during the trip we made, we were able to appreciate how much NATO has done to maintain peace in Europe. That does not mean that NATO will be in a position to continue playing such an important role. However, in view of the stability which prevailed in the countries protected by NATO, we must acknowledge that, for all practical purposes, only the older countries and especially those of Asia, have enjoyed a certain degree of peace and have been able to rebuild their economies. It has been my privilege to realize that Canada has played a useful role in the sense that it has created in the minds of Europeans a spirit
54S8

Supply-National Defence which enabled them to rebuild their economy because they felt truly protected by their allies.
On the other hand, one can ask whether the maintenance cost of these units in Europe is warranted. It would therefore be wise to make a comparison with the one who pays for a fire insurance. Were he sure that no fire would break out, he would not incur such an expense. However, everyone of us is glad to pay a premium in order to have protection against any fire hazards. We make sacrifices in order to feel protected.
Up to now, what we have paid to NATO may have seemed forbidding, but I believe that it has amounted somewhat to an insurance premium which allowed us to live in a state of relative peacefulness, to generate a certain understanding among the peoples of Europe, and to induce at the same time the lessening of tension which we now enjoy.
The role this committee has to play is not to analyse what has been done in the past so much as to supervise what is being done at the present time, and in the light of acquired knowledge, to endeavour to determine what part Canada should play in the military field, in years to come. We have concluded agreements, whether they have been signed or not they are none the less agreements and, as gentlemen, we must honour them as long as conditions upon which they are based remain the same.
I think that we have agreements and that as long as these agreements last it is unlikely that the situation will change.
But we may anticipate that before a few years, perhaps three, four or even five years, the military situation will have changed enough to enable us to depart to a certain extent from the role we now play in Europe.
I do not think I would anticipate the forthcoming report of the committee if I made this remark, since the forces of France, Germany and other European countries are being restored day after day. If we consider that Germany, only in the last few years, set up a military force about 380,000 strong, I feel it is logical to conclude that in future we will play a token role in Europe to show our willingness to participate and our solidarity with our European allies.
However, we noticed that most of our servicemen in Europe seem to be satisfied with their living conditions. We noticed also the high degree of efficiency achieved by our military forces.
However, we were rather alarmed to learn that possible repatriation of our servicemen's dependents who are now in Europe, has not been considered in the event of war. I am of the opinion that the government should give

its attention to this problem and find a solution to safeguard the security of Canadian civilians who are now in Europe with our servicemen.
In the introduction of his department's estimates today, the Minister of National Defence stated that he was contemplating a substantial reduction in the expenditures of his department by closing a great number of auxiliary bases and reducing the military forces.
Referring to his statement, we can conclude that the most affected will be the Royal Canadian Air Force. I do not think the minister is wrong in considering a reduction of amounts assigned to air forces. If we consider the development of arms which are now used, which are a threat to peace, it is sensible to conclude that the part assigned to the air forces will gradually decrease because the future threat seems to lie, for many years to come, in the availability to the two contending camps of nuclear weapons carried by guided missiles and nuclear submarines carrying Polaris missiles.
This, Mr. Chairman, leads me to the conclusion that, if we believe that Canada has a nuclear role to play, I think that it would be more logical if this role were to be a contribution to the cost of the expenditures resulting from the maintenance of the retaliation force that we have at present in the west.
It has been admitted, from all the evidence gathered, that there is no adequate defence system as such, and that our retaliatory power alone has been able up to now to maintain peace.
I am of the opinion, unless I have proof to the contrary and until other armament are produced, that we must stand by this acknowledgement of the facts. I submit that it is of no avail to allocate the nation's credits for military defence establishments which, after all, have no value.
Turning back to the announcement made by the Minister of National Defence to the effect that he will reduce the strength of some military establishments, 1 shall point out to him that all Canadians wish for a reduction of military expenditures. Besides, all members have expressed that wish.
All responsible economic bodies also wish that the government would reduce its military expenditures in order to balance its budget.
But, when the Minister of National Defence announces these reductions, some people seem to be personally affected and they rebel. I think that these people follow the theory by which when others are affected and they are not, they are satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure the minister that I myself and the members of my group, fully agree that we should work together towards reducing the amounts allocated for military purposes. But we must also take into account the fact that if we increase unemployment by reducing the amounts allocated for the defence of our country, we prove beyond any doubt that since the end of the war in 1945 we have maintained, without any good reason, an economic system based too much, unfortunately, on a military economy which, today, plunges us in a small economic crisis which seems to be only starting and which will no doubt be felt in various areas in our country.
It is unfortunate that such a thing should happen, but I think the present government will have to realize that it cannot reduce expenditures, thus creating some unemployment, without putting into effect at the same time a clear program devised to create jobs resulting solely from the industrial and economic growth of our country and from the development of our natural resources, since these are the only areas on which we can safely depend.
As a matter of fact, it is toward those sectors that European countries have directed all their efforts, since the end of the last conflict, and we have been able to appreciate the happy results achieved thereby.
Mr. Chairman, I believe we must consider that military problem in terms of the future, in the light of the changing relations between the various countries of the world.
If we study the economic philosophies which are put forth at the present time throughout the world, we can divide them in three groups.
First, there is the controlled economy of the totalitarian communist states, such as Russia and her satellites.
Then, there is the controlled economy which could be described as a modified socialist economy and which is to be found in central Europe. And we have here, in the west, the capitalist system.
I think those three philosophies will evolve. The two extremes will attract each other, which means that the communist group will evolve in the same direction as the central European group, towards a mitigated socialism. On the other hand, we, in the west, shall evolve in the same way, as, with the passing of the years, a multiplication of contacts, relations and travel between the various nations of the world will tend to erase boundaries.
I think we shall have to take up the challenge of a cold economic war, if we want to keep abreast of our responsibilities and that
Supply-National Defence we shall have to consider a scheme for the development of energizing countries. This scheme should benefit those countries, and not the capitalist colonizing nations, as was the case in the past. We shall do it as a friendly country putting its technological knowledge at the disposal of people who cannot look after themselves.
Moreover, I am of the opinion that the amount of money we proposed to take from military establishment should be, to a certain extent, given to religious organizations, because I always think that in underdeveloped countries, the organizations which are best suited to help those regions are the semireligious organizations that are on the spot and which, with the men at their disposal, can help those people to develop and to take their responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member who preceded me when he said that in the years to come, we shall see the various people in the world united.
In closing my remarks, I want to tell the house my personal impression with regard to that infernal contraption we call nuclear arms: those arms which we have cursed since their creation, that is for the past 18 years, I think, that we shall soon bless them, because they will contribute to restore somewhat the sense of responsibility of national leaders who, nowadays, may not take any uncompromising or irresponsible decision nor plunge their people into wars.
Mr. Chairman, the day is probably not far when we shall thank those who have created that infernal machine because it shall contribute to safeguard us from the blunders of a few invidious, a few proud people, such as others before us have known in the centuries and years past and whose decisions these have dearly paid.
Some pretend we may be able to ban those weapons. I say no, that we shall not be able to ban them because, even if we wanted to, I am sure if there were a conflict in which conventional arms would be used for a few weeks, if not a few months, later on, we would see those weapons reappear. We have them; let us look at them with their power of destruction, let us look at them with that bit of wisdom they are forcing on us, for they make us realize to what extent we are irresponsible when we plunge our peoples into war.
Mr. Chairman, with these last words, I am ready to allow the house to adjourn.

Mr. Chairman, may I first congratulate the minister on his appointment and wish him well. I should also like to congratulate the previous speaker. I thought his was an excellent presentation, sensible, logical, and at least slightly patriotic. I wish I could say the same for some of the preceding speakers, particularly the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria. He mentioned Cape Breton very often, but how few were his references to Canada.
I come from a very small province, probably the poorest, and we need many things. We have not got a $30 million heavy water installation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: You have Smallwood over there, which is why you don't have anything.

It is because we have Mr. Smallwood we have what we have. Mr. Chairman, it will be obvious I regret very much the decision of the Department of National Defence, especially with regard to Torbay, Newfoundland. It is particularly hard because this department has never had a very heavy investment in my province, despite the fact that we are right off the Atlantic and are the actual Gibraltar of the continent. Our defence installations were mainly American. But, we are not an unreasonable people. We know that the minister has had to make unpleasant decisions, but surely the Canadian taxpayers generally will be glad to learn that some of the unnecessary defence expenditure will be cut out. This, of course, is a very laudable course of action, if at the same time we do not jeopardize our national security.
We of St. John's have no illusions that money grows on trees. Far from it; we know the government must find the money for equalization payments to the provinces. In this respect, Newfoundland will receive well over an additional $3 million. We know someone must

pay for an increase in the old age pension, in the blind pension, in old age assistance and in the disabled persons' pension.
We know that the federal government is now paying 90 per cent of the cost of completing our sorely needed trans-Canada highway. But the fact remains that the economy of my city cannot help but be affected in some way. St. John's, and indeed all of Newfoundland, asks the federal government to aid us in the development of our city and our province, and we do not ask as a pauper.
It might be of interest to some hon. members to realize that Newfoundland, if you think of it as a separate entity, as it was before 1949, is now Canada's third biggest customer, exceeded only by the United States and Great Britain. So, we ask for development, not for charity. Therefore this temporary setback on defence installation places a greater onus on the government to approach the problem of unemployment with even yet more vigour.
What will happen to the men who lose their jobs-the men who will be out of work? Surely some extra attention and consideration must be paid to them. An extra effort to find them alternative employment must be, and I am quite sure, will be made. Perhaps as a result of this very decision the acute problem of unemployment in my district, and in all Canada, will be brought to the attention of the government more forcefully. Perhaps, too, the Minister of National Defence will understand, if we look to him for sympathy and support when other proposals to assist my province are brought to the government.
Already we have had at least one department of defence ship come to our drydock in St. John's, the first in many years. I wonder if the minister, as a result of his difficult decision today, could not lend his weight to greater use of this drydock by the ships of our Canadian navy, and to a greater use of our harbour by ships of every department? The people of St. John's will understand this decision, but only if they see that the money so saved by the department will be put to other, more worth-while usage.
Indeed we hope the government will soon increase the family allowance, and soon keep our promise that this allowance will be paid so long as students remain at school. If this announcement of the minister will make this decision with regard to family allowance come sooner, then many will applaud.
Surely too, this unfavourable decision puts a greater onus on the federal government to launch an all-out attack to find a solution to the Bell Island problem. There are no doubt numerous valid ways in which the federal government could spend constructively in Newfoundland, and in the other nine

provinces. Therefore, if the experts tell us that we are spending this money uneconomically we are the first to want a change, because in our province as in others, there are many ways in which this money can be spent profitably, and if this cutback will mean this money will be spent more profitably in other ways, then we support it.
I have one last word, and it is that I hope the government is taking every possible step to ease the effects of this decision on the persons actually laid off. I would like to know just what consideration has been given to their investments in pension plans. I would like to know if any consideration has been given to ease any financial problems placed on those who have mortgage payments to meet and who might be required to move elsewhere.
I would also request the Minister of Labour to send a special representative from the national employment service at once, to assist in finding alternative jobs. I suggest that this be an extra assistance over and above that normally given. While we understand, we regret the necessity for this decision and, as a result of it, we will expect some extra effort be made to compensate for its temporary ill effects.

Wealthy in brains; not like yourself.
A party of bureaucrats.

speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member resume his seat, please. The remarks being made are not perhaps conducive to the good order of the house and I would ask hon. members on both sides of the house to concentrate on the item that is before the committee at the moment.

I appreciate your thinking on the matter, Mr. Chairman, but as I heard that remark it was very personal and I think the hon. member who made it should

rise and withdraw it; or if he cares to repeat it, I will see what I can do about handling it at a later time.
I will continue with my remarks. One of the first remarks made by the Minister of National Defence this afternoon was nothing less than a complete denial of the words his own Prime Minister spoke previously in the house. With regard to the defence committee, everybody is well aware of the fact that when the defence committee was set up the words of the Prime Minister at that time were that the committee was to look into all aspects-I repeat, all aspects-of defence matters. This afternoon the Minister of National Defence referred to the committee as looking into "various matters". This is exactly what has taken place. This committee is unlike committees set up by other allied nations which have defence committees. All such committees working under other governments have the opportunity to examine every bit of evidence that is available, including classified information. But this minister and this government have denied the committee set up by this house-and they made a big noise about setting it up- classified information; and well they might, when they consider what the present minister did while in opposition. This is the minister who I consider individually is the greatest threat to security in this country. And why do I say that?
Louder.

If you are having trouble, go wash out your ears. I say it because the opportunity to seek classified information was open to him while in opposition. This same minister, with his arrogant attitude, came before this house and is recorded in Hansard as having said he could not understand why it was classified and he was going to take the responsibility of repeating it. If that is not a security risk, I do not know what it is. It is a security risk for which in other free countries he would be placed behind bars.
Oh, oh.

They are "oh'ing" and
"ah'ing" over there. It is rather nasty of me to say this, but this is a nasty situation. This afternoon hon. members referred to the minister's decision as brave; they said it was a brave decision. It is a gutless decision; because when he was in opposition he had all the answers and all the cures, and what he has brought forward now is sickening. It is not a cure; it is a sickness. Why do I say it is a sickness? This minister is aware of the situation with our allies in the NATO set-up. I defy any member of the defence committee,

any member of that party or any member on that front bench, to rise and deny that the attitude in defence among the allies today is one of the deterrent, and the deterrent is made up of nothing but tactical weapons, I.C.B.M.'s and the like. In other words, the approach of the allies on the matter of defence boils down to nothing but "a good offence is the best defence." These are all offensive weapons held as deterrents in order to prevent an outbreak of war in any part of the world. I say again, they are offensive weapons.
If the minister wants to make a brave decision, to which he and his government have already committed themselves, why not get rid of the Bomarc? I say that for the reason that the Bomarc is nothing but a defensive weapon with a very short range. Its capabilities have been discussed before the committee, and every capability of the Bomarc has been questioned from one source or another. As a defensive weapon it does not belong in the arsenal of the NATO countries. They are depending upon tactical nuclear weapons, I.C.B.M.'s and the like. In addition to that, the savings-as I followed the minister's remarks this afternoon: I did not have too much opportunity to add up the particular savings-of maintaining the Bomarc I understand will be in the vicinity of $37 million. I should say, of keeping the Bomarc, because after all this was a housekeeping presentation which the minister made. Not counting maintenance and other costs involved I understand it is in the vicinity of $9 million a year. What about the other facilities involved? Owing to the fact that the Bomarc is still not armed with nuclear warheads, why does the minister not make a brave decision? The government had already committed itself to negotiating out of the agreement and doing away with the Bomarc, so possibly we could salvage something from the cut-backs he has made today.
The minister talks about withdrawing ten ships from naval duties. After withdrawing them he then maintains there will still be adequate support for the fleet. I would ask the minister to explain who gave him such advice. He has already announced the scrapping of the frigate program. We have heard the former minister of defence speak about this program and at the time he was minister it was considered a substantial program for the next 20 years. Who is advising the minister to make these cut-backs, and why? It is not the navy which advised the cut-back of the frigate program. Admiral Rayner appeared before the committee and gave his thoughts on the matter. Yet the minister decides to withdraw from the frigate program 28902-5-351}
Supply-National Defence and now says that ten ships are to be withdrawn from the navy. It is very surprising that this minister made that decision in face of this advice from the senior admiral in the navy. It might also surprise the minister to know that this was a program in which the British government were very much interested. I call his attention to the committee reports of what was told us while in Britain by the upper echelons of the British defence department, wherein he will find an indication that the United Kingdom were very much interested in this program. They would not have been interested in the frigate program, Mr. Chairman, unless that particular program had merit, because I cannot imagine the British wasting their time on this program unless it was thought a worth-while one.
So here we have a minister who had failed to advise the committee where he is getting his advice on these matters. The minister said on one occasion that a remark he made before the committee did not show up as such in the committee reports, but the same minister has the audacity, in view of remarks he made when he was on this side of the house, to suggest we forget the remarks which he made in respect of defence. We were supposed to time the matter by the calendar, but I prefer the watch. Since it is the minister's advice that we should forget what he said about defence I will continue to forget it, because in my opinion he does not know very much about what is going on, in view of the fact that he is defying advice of a senior admiral with respect to the frigate program. Now he has branched off on this cut-back program. As I say the government has committed itself to negotiate out of the Bomarc problem-and it is a problem, because it does nothing for the defence of North America.
The hon. member for Vancouver East referred to what Mr. McNamara said about the Bomarcs, and we know what his intentions were. On one occasion he said it was a decoy. This minister is the same hon. member who on many occasions concerned himself about Canada's image abroad. His great slogan was: "Save Canada's image abroad". It appears to me that to save Canada's image abroad today calls for a very big sacrifice. It calls for the sacrifice of the personal image of Canada and Canada's own integrity. The government have considered nothing of their attitudes on defence and other matters in respect to the people of Canada; they only try to continue to pull the wool over people's eyes in respect of matters they consider in the honour of Canada's image abroad.
I would not want it thought for one moment, Mr. Chairman, that we are not grateful

Supply-National Defence for the very small part the federal government has played in announcing the fact that the government will purchase heavy water from Cape Breton. I know this news was gratefully accepted in Cape Breton, and I myself am grateful for it. However, as was said earlier this evening, the government gives you something with one hand and takes away twice as much with the other. While I am at it, I might also say a lot has been said by other hon. members about the heavy water plant going to Nova Scotia. One hon. member said that it cost $13 a ton in Nova Scotia to mine coal whereas it could be mined in his area for $3. There must have been a strong profit motive involved, if heavy water could be produced using coal that much cheaper than in Cape Breton, when they did not underbid Nova Scotia to begin with. I am very grateful that this particular project is coming to Cape Breton, but whatever benefits it may have to Cape Breton or Nova Scotia have been offset by what happened here today.
